topics.title: Meet the story: Daudet, Alsace and a late morning

learn.hook: Imagine waking up to find that from tomorrow your school may not teach in your own language. That is the morning Franz walks into.
points: Author: Alphonse Daudet, a French novelist and short-story writer of the 19th century.
Background: the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71. Prussia, led by Bismarck, defeated France and took the border districts of Alsace and Lorraine.
Narrator: Franz, a young schoolboy in a village of Alsace, tells the story in the first person, looking back on that day.
Opening: Franz is late and dreads being questioned on participles, which he has not learnt at all.
Temptation: the warm bright day, birds chirping at the edge of the woods and Prussian soldiers drilling in the field behind the sawmill pull him outdoors, but he resists and hurries to school.

example.q: Why does Daudet open the story with Franz being late and unprepared?
steps: Franz's fear of the participle test shows how little he cares for French lessons.
This careless attitude sets up a strong contrast with his deep regret later.
So the opening prepares the reader for the change in Franz.
example.answer: It shows Franz as a careless boy at first, so that his later remorse over losing French lessons feels sharper.

learn.reallife: Many Indian students skip a regional-language class thinking it is 'easy marks later'. Franz learns, too late, that a language can be taken away.

topics.title: An unusual morning at school

learn.hook: Picture your noisy classroom gone silent like a Sunday, and your strictest teacher smiling at you. Something is very wrong.
points: At the town hall a crowd stands before the bulletin board; for two years all the bad news (lost battles, the draft, the commanding officer's orders) had come from there.
Usually school begins with a great bustle: desks banging, lessons repeated aloud in unison, the teacher's ruler rapping on the table. Franz had hoped to slip in unseen under that noise.
That day it is as quiet as a Sunday morning. Franz expects a scolding, but M. Hamel kindly tells him to go to his place.
M. Hamel is in his Sunday best: his beautiful green coat, frilled shirt and little black silk cap, all embroidered, worn only on inspection and prize days.
Village elders sit silently on the back benches: old Hauser with his old primer, the former mayor and the former postmaster.

example.q: List three things that were unusual at school that day.
steps: Recall the normal routine: noise, bustle, ruler on the table.
Compare: it was silent, M. Hamel was gentle, he wore his special clothes.
Add the villagers sitting on the back benches.
example.answer: The silence, M. Hamel's kindness and best clothes, and the village elders on the back benches.

learn.reallife: When something big happens, Indians crowd around notice boards, from exam results to railway charts. In Franz's village, the notice board brought news of war.

topics.title: The order from Berlin and Franz's regret

learn.hook: One line on a notice can change a whole people's future. M. Hamel reads it out in a trembling voice.
points: M. Hamel announces the order from Berlin: only German is to be taught in the schools of Alsace and Lorraine.
This is their last French lesson; the new master arrives the next day.
Franz is shocked that he can hardly write French. He regrets hunting birds' eggs and sliding on the Saar; his grammar and history books now feel like old friends.
When Franz fails to recite the participle rule, M. Hamel does not scold him. He says that Alsace's great trouble is putting off learning till tomorrow.
He blames everyone: parents sent children to work on farms or in mills for a little more money, and he himself sent pupils to water his flowers or gave a holiday when he wanted to go fishing.

example.q: How did the order from Berlin change Franz's feelings about his books?
steps: Before: the books were a nuisance and heavy to carry.
After the order: he could lose French lessons forever.
So the books suddenly felt like old friends he could not bear to give up.
example.answer: His once-boring grammar and history books became like old friends he could not give up.

learn.reallife: Families sometimes pull children out of school to help earn money, as M. Hamel says Alsatian parents did. Laws like the Right to Education Act in India try to stop exactly this loss.

topics.title: The last lesson itself

learn.hook: Ever noticed you understand a lesson perfectly on the day you know it is the last revision? That is what happens to Franz.
points: M. Hamel calls French the most beautiful language in the world, the clearest and the most logical, and asks them to guard it.
His key idea: when a people are enslaved, holding on to their language is like holding the key to their prison.
Grammar, then writing and history follow. Franz understands everything. New copies saying 'France, Alsace' hang from the desks like little flags.
Pigeons coo on the roof, and Franz wonders whether they too will be made to sing in German.
At twelve the church clock strikes, the Angelus rings and Prussian trumpets sound. Too moved to speak, M. Hamel writes 'Vive La France!' on the board and dismisses the class.

example.q: Explain: 'as long as they hold fast to their language it is as if they had the key to their prison' (paraphrase).
steps: Prison here means being ruled by a conqueror.
Language keeps a people's identity, culture and unity alive.
So a people who keep their language can one day win back their freedom.
example.answer: Language preserves identity, and with it the hope and means to regain freedom; it is the key to escaping foreign rule.

learn.reallife: India's freedom struggle used songs, newspapers and slogans in many Indian languages to unite people. Language kept the idea of freedom alive, just as M. Hamel says.

topics.title: Characters, mother tongue and linguistic chauvinism

learn.hook: Some people learn the value of something only when it is snatched away. Every main character in this story does.
points: Franz: careless and playful at first; then remorseful, sensitive and suddenly eager to learn.
M. Hamel: strict but devoted teacher of forty years; patriotic and deeply emotional at the end.
Villagers: they come to the class full of regret for not learning their language when they had the chance.
Mother tongue: it carries a people's identity, memory and culture; losing it is losing a part of oneself.
Linguistic chauvinism: forcing one's language on others, or treating other languages as inferior. Here the conquerors impose German on Alsace and Lorraine.

example.q: Is the Prussian order an example of linguistic chauvinism? Give a reason.
steps: Define it: aggressive pride in one's language and imposing it on others.
The order bans French and forces German on a conquered people.
So it fits the definition exactly.
example.answer: Yes. The conquerors force German on Alsace and Lorraine and deny people their own language.

learn.reallife: India has 22 languages in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution. Respecting every language, rather than forcing one, keeps such a diverse nation together.

topics.title: Themes and craft: delay, patriotism, irony and symbols

learn.hook: 'Kal kare so aaj kar' (do tomorrow's work today) runs Kabir's famous doha. Daudet's whole story is a painful lesson in that line.
points: Procrastination: the habit of putting off learning till tomorrow; M. Hamel calls it the great trouble of Alsace.
Patriotism and loss: the pain of war appears in the bulletin board, the silent class and Hamel's breakdown.
First-person narration makes Franz's feelings direct and personal.
Irony: the 'last' lesson turns out to be the best lesson Franz ever had; he understands everything only when it is too late.
Symbols and pathos: the bulletin board (bad news), the pigeons (absurd imposition), 'Vive La France!' (undying patriotism), with vivid, moving description.

example.q: Explain the irony in the title 'The Last Lesson'.
steps: Irony is a contrast between what is expected and what happens.
Franz never cared for lessons, yet the final one is the one he understands best.
The people value French only when it is about to be taken away.
example.answer: The last lesson becomes the most meaningful one; value is realised only at the moment of loss.

learn.reallife: Exam toppers often say, 'Start revision early.' Board students who delay till the last week feel exactly what Franz felt about French.

topics.title: Words from the lesson and the past perfect

learn.hook: 'Tycoon' comes from Japan and 'robot' from Czech. English is a borrower, and this lesson asks you to trace its loans.
points: Phrases from the text: 'in great dread of' (very afraid of), 'counted on' (relied on), 'thumbing the pages' (turning pages with the thumb), 'a great bustle' (busy noise), 'reproach ourselves with' (blame ourselves for).
Word origins: tycoon (Japanese, 'great lord'), tulip (Turkish word for turban), logo (Greek 'logos', word), zero (Arabic 'sifr'), trek (Dutch/Afrikaans, to travel), robot (Czech), bandicoot (Telugu).
Choose a meaning from context: read the whole sentence and pick the sense that fits.
Past perfect (had + past participle) shows the earlier of two past actions, e.g. 'I had counted on the noise to reach my desk unseen.'

example.q: Combine using the past perfect: Franz reached school. The lesson began before that.
steps: Identify the earlier action: the lesson began.
Put the earlier action in the past perfect: had begun.
Keep the later action in the simple past: reached.
example.answer: When Franz reached school, the lesson had already begun.

learn.reallife: Many English words come from Indian languages too: 'jungle', 'shampoo', 'bungalow', 'pyjamas'. Language borrowing shows how cultures meet.

topics.title: Board exam practice: The Last Lesson

learn.hook: Board examiners love this story. A sharp 40–50 word answer on M. Hamel or Franz can be your easiest marks.
points: Short answers (40–50 words): make one clear point, support it with one detail from the text, and end with its significance.
Common 'think as you read' questions: what Franz expected, what was unusual, what was on the bulletin board, what changed after the order, how Franz's feelings changed.
Long answers (120–150 words): for 'importance of mother tongue', use the key-to-the-prison idea, the villagers' regret and the theme of identity.
Discussion questions: peoples who lost their languages, problems of linguistic minorities, and whether pride in language can go too far (linguistic chauvinism).

example.q: Draft a 40–50 word answer: How did the people realise the value of their language?
steps: Point: they realised its value only when it was being taken away.
Evidence: villagers sat in the class; Franz regretted wasted time.
Significance: they understood language is their identity.
example.answer: When the order from Berlin banned French, villagers came to the last lesson full of regret and Franz wished he had studied. Losing French made them see that their language was their identity and the key to their freedom.

learn.reallife: Debates on mother-tongue education in India, as in the NEP 2020 emphasis on home language in early years, echo the questions this story raises.

topics.title: Saheb of Seemapuri: garbage and wonder

learn.hook: Every morning, before most of Delhi wakes, children with sacks on their shoulders are already searching through the city's garbage. Anees Jung asks them why.
points: Author: Anees Jung, an Indian journalist and writer. The chapter is an extract from her book 'Lost Spring: Stories of Stolen Childhood'.
Form: a two-part reportage on child labour and poverty: Part 1 on Saheb, a ragpicker in Delhi; Part 2 on Mukesh, a bangle-maker's son in Firozabad.
Saheb-e-Alam's family came from Dhaka, Bangladesh, after storms swept away their fields and homes.
They live in Seemapuri, on the outskirts of Delhi, in mud structures with roofs of tin and tarpaulin, without sewage, drainage or running water.
For the elders ragpicking is a means of survival; for the children garbage is wrapped in wonder, because they may find a coin or even a ten-rupee note.

example.q: Why does the author say garbage means different things to children and to elders?
steps: Elders depend on what they collect to feed the family: survival.
Children are thrilled by the chance of finding a coin: wonder.
So the same garbage is a hard job for one and a treasure hunt for the other.
example.answer: For elders it is a means of survival; for children it holds the wonder of a possible find, like a coin.

learn.reallife: India's National Child Labour Project and the Right to Education Act (free schooling for ages 6–14) aim to move children like Saheb from rag sacks to school bags.

topics.title: Barefoot, a grand name and a lost freedom

learn.hook: A boy named 'Lord of the Universe' cannot afford a pair of chappals. Anees Jung lets that irony speak for itself.
points: Many children walk barefoot. Some say it is a tradition, but the author suspects this explains away constant poverty.
Saheb-e-Alam means 'lord of the universe', ironic for a barefoot boy who picks rags.
The author jokingly asks if he would go to school if she started one; days later he asks if her school is ready, and she feels embarrassed by her empty promise.
Later Saheb works at a tea stall for 800 rupees and all his meals. He now carries a steel canister instead of his plastic bag.
He has lost his freedom: the bag was his, but the canister belongs to the tea-stall owner. He is no longer his own master.

example.q: Is Saheb happier at the tea stall? Explain.
steps: He earns 800 rupees and gets meals, so he is better fed.
But his carefree look is gone; the steel canister feels heavier than the bag.
The bag was his own; now he works for a master.
example.answer: No. He earns more, but he has lost his freedom and carefree spirit; he is no longer his own master.

learn.reallife: Thousands of children still work at dhabas and tea stalls in India. Their wages may seem like progress, but the cost is their childhood and schooling.

topics.title: Firozabad: the bangle makers

learn.hook: Bright glass bangles jingle at weddings across India. Few buyers think of the dark rooms where they are made.
points: Mukesh lives in Firozabad, the centre of India's glass-bangle industry.
About 20,000 children work near high-temperature furnaces and glass-blowing units in dingy cells without air and light; many lose their eyesight before they become adults.
Child labour is illegal, yet it thrives; families have made bangles for generations.
Savita, a young girl in a drab pink dress, solders pieces of glass beside an elderly woman.
Bangles symbolise a married Indian woman's auspiciousness (suhaag); Savita may not yet know the sanctity of what she is making.

example.q: Why is there irony in Savita making bangles?
steps: Bangles are a symbol of a married woman's good fortune.
Savita is a young girl working in grim conditions, not enjoying any such fortune.
She makes symbols of joy while her own childhood is lost.
example.answer: She makes the symbols of a happy married life while her own life is joyless labour.

learn.reallife: Studies of the Firozabad glass industry have long reported eye and lung problems among workers. Safety rules and bans on child labour exist, but enforcement is the real challenge.

topics.title: The vicious circle and Mukesh's dream

learn.hook: Imagine making something beautiful all your life and never once eating a full meal. An old bangle maker lives that truth.
points: An elderly woman says she has not enjoyed even one full meal in her whole life, though she has made bangles throughout it.
The workers are trapped in a vicious circle of sahukars (moneylenders), middlemen, policemen, keepers of the law, bureaucrats and politicians.
They cannot organise: if they did, they fear being hauled up by the police, beaten and jailed; there is no leader and no cooperative.
Mukesh is different. He dreams of being a motor mechanic and driving a car, a dream that breaks away from the family tradition of bangle making.

example.q: Why does the author see Mukesh's dream as hopeful?
steps: Everyone around him accepts bangle making as destiny.
Mukesh wants to be a motor mechanic and learn to drive a car.
Choosing his own path shows courage to break the circle.
example.answer: His dream to be a motor mechanic breaks away from the inherited trade, showing courage and hope.

learn.reallife: Self-help groups and cooperatives, like those under India's DAY-NRLM mission, help artisans sell without middlemen. That is exactly what the bangle workers lacked.

topics.title: Themes, the title, and answer writing

learn.hook: Spring is the season of new leaves. Childhood is the spring of life. What happens when a child never gets one?
points: Child labour and the loss of childhood: children like Saheb and Savita work instead of playing and learning.
Poverty and exploitation, made worse by the burden of tradition and fate (karam), which people accept without question.
Hope: Mukesh's dream and Saheb's interest in school show that the wish for a better life survives.
Title metaphor: 'spring' stands for childhood; 'lost spring' means childhood stolen by poverty and work.
Answer writing: short answers (40–50 words) on Saheb or Mukesh need one key point plus a detail; a long answer on child labour should cover causes, effects and solutions.

example.q: Explain the title 'Lost Spring' in about 40 words.
steps: Spring = youth, freshness, growth = childhood.
Saheb and Mukesh lose this stage to labour and poverty.
So their 'spring' is lost.
example.answer: Spring symbolises childhood. Saheb and Mukesh lose the joys of childhood, like play and school, to poverty and labour, so the title means 'stolen childhood'.

learn.reallife: India's 2011 Census counted about one crore working children aged 5–14. Every one of those numbers is a 'lost spring'.

topics.title: Craft and questions: reportage, irony, and the role of society

learn.hook: A news report gives numbers. A reportage like this gives names, faces and voices, and that is why you remember it.
points: Reportage technique: first-hand observation, real names, dialogue ('Is your school ready?') and vivid imagery.
Irony: Saheb's grand name against his poverty; bright, colourful bangles against the grim lives of their makers.

Think-as-you-read answers: Saheb looks for coins in garbage; he lives in Seemapuri because storms drove his family from Dhaka; children go barefoot because of poverty; Saheb is not happy at the tea stall because he has lost his freedom.
Understanding the text: Mukesh dreams of being a motor mechanic; the bangle industry harms eyesight; workers cannot organise for fear of the police and lack of a cooperative.
Society's role: enforce child-labour laws, provide schools, form cooperatives and spread awareness among buyers.

example.q: How does the author make the reader feel Saheb's reality, not just know about it?
steps: She uses his real name and its meaning.
She quotes his words and her own.
She describes Seemapuri in concrete detail: mud, tin, tarpaulin.
example.answer: Through real names, dialogue and vivid concrete detail, typical of reportage.

topics.title: Douglas and the first fear of water

learn.hook: A future judge of the most powerful court in the USA was once a skinny boy who froze in a swimming pool. This is his true story.
points: Author: William O. Douglas, a Judge of the US Supreme Court and an environmentalist. 'Deep Water' is an extract from his autobiography 'Of Men and Mountains'.
Form: an autobiographical, first-person account of a childhood fear of water and how he conquered it.
First fear: at three or four, on a California beach with his father, the waves knocked him down and swept over him; he was buried in water and frightened.
At ten or eleven he decided to learn to swim at the YMCA pool in Yakima, because it was safer than the river his mother warned him about. He used water wings at first.
The pool's shallow end was about three feet deep; the deep end was about nine feet.

example.q: Why did Douglas choose the YMCA pool and not the Yakima River?
steps: His mother kept warning him that the river was treacherous.
The pool was considered safe, with a shallow end of about three feet.
So the YMCA pool was the sensible place to begin.
example.answer: The river was dangerous and his mother warned him against it, while the YMCA pool was safe.

learn.reallife: Many Indian children first learn to swim in a municipal pool, often with floats like Douglas's water wings, before trying rivers or the sea, which are much less predictable.

topics.title: The misadventure at the YMCA pool

learn.hook: A big boy's idea of a joke at a swimming pool can leave a scar of fear for years.
points: A big bruiser of a boy, about eighteen, called him 'Skinny', picked him up and tossed him into the deep end.
Douglas swallowed water and sank. On the way down he planned to make a big jump from the bottom, come up and paddle to the edge.
The nine feet felt like ninety. He rose slowly and sank again; this happened three times.
Stark terror: his legs felt paralysed, he tried to scream but no sound came out, and he saw only yellowish water.
At last he stopped struggling, felt calm and peaceful, and blacked out. He woke up lying beside the pool, vomiting.

example.q: Trace the change in Douglas's state of mind while he was drowning.
steps: First: frightened but still able to plan a jump from the bottom.
Then: panic and terror as the plan failed and his legs froze.
Finally: he stopped struggling, felt peace, and blacked out.
example.answer: Fear with a plan, then sheer panic and terror, then calm peace before he lost consciousness.

learn.reallife: Lifeguards in Indian pools are trained to watch for 'silent drowning': a drowning person often cannot shout, just as Douglas could not scream.

topics.title: A fear that stayed, and a teacher with a rope

learn.hook: Some fears pass in a day. Douglas's lasted for years, until he decided enough was enough.
points: A haunting fear of water stayed with him for years; whenever he entered water, his legs would freeze and terror would grip him.
It spoiled his joys: whenever he waded in the Tieton or the Bumping River, or bathed in Warm Lake, terror gripped him; it also ruined his fishing trips and the fun of canoeing, boating and swimming.
He resolved to conquer the fear because it was ruining his enjoyment of life.
He hired an instructor who trained him for months, five days a week, an hour a day.
The method: a belt around his waist, attached to a rope that ran through a pulley on an overhead cable. The instructor held the rope and walked him back and forth across the pool.

example.q: Why did Douglas finally decide to hire an instructor?
steps: The fear stopped him from canoeing, bathing and fishing.
It was ruining the fun of outdoor life he loved.
So he resolved to overcome it with expert help.
example.answer: Because his fear was spoiling activities he loved, like canoeing and fishing, he resolved to conquer it.

learn.reallife: Indian swimming coaches still use similar methods, like a rope or a pole held by the coach, so that a frightened learner feels safe while building skill.

topics.title: Building a swimmer, piece by piece

learn.hook: Big skills are built from small parts. Douglas's instructor broke swimming into tiny steps.
points: Step-by-step training: put the face under water and exhale; raise the nose and inhale; repeat many times.
Next: hold the side of the pool and kick with the legs; then combine arms, legs and breathing into a whole stroke. 'Piece by piece he built a swimmer.'
Even after training, small traces of terror returned when he swam alone, so he kept swimming to beat them.
Test 1: at Lake Wentworth in New Hampshire, he dived off a dock and swam two miles across the lake. The terror tried to return once, but he swam on.
Test 2: at Warm Lake he dived in, swam across to the other shore and back, and shouted with joy. The terror was gone.

example.q: Why did Douglas test himself at Lake Wentworth and Warm Lake after the training?
steps: The instructor's work was done, but traces of fear remained.
He needed to be sure he could swim alone in deep, open water.
Swimming across and back at Warm Lake proved the terror was gone.
example.answer: To be sure the last traces of fear had gone, he swam alone in open lakes; at Warm Lake he knew he had won.

learn.reallife: Cricketers practise in nets ball by ball before facing a real match. Douglas did the same with breathing, kicking and strokes before facing open lakes.

topics.title: Themes: fear, the will to live and freedom

learn.hook: 'All we have to fear is fear itself.' Douglas borrowed a president's words to sum up a boy's victory.
points: Fear can paralyse a person, but it can be overcome by willpower, patience and practice.
Douglas quotes US President Franklin D. Roosevelt: 'All we have to fear is fear itself.' The fear of something is often worse than the thing.
Near death he felt peace; afterwards his will to live grew stronger. He says there is terror only in the fear of death.
Victory over fear brings freedom: he could enjoy rivers, lakes and mountains again.

example.q: Explain 'All we have to fear is fear itself' with reference to Douglas.

Once he faced and beat the fear, the water held no danger for him.
example.answer: His fear, not the water, was his real enemy; by conquering it, he was free.

learn.reallife: Top Indian athletes often talk about beating nerves before a big final. Mastering the fear is often the real contest.

topics.title: Craft and vocabulary of Deep Water

learn.hook: Read the drowning scene and you almost hold your breath. That is the power of sensory writing.
points: Sensory description: yellowish water, choking, frozen legs; repetition of going down and coming up builds suspense.
Tone: reflective; the adult Douglas looks back calmly. Strong contrast between helplessness in the pool and triumph at Warm Lake.

Vocabulary: bruiser (big, tough person), flailed (waved wildly), paralysed (unable to move), misadventure (unlucky accident), stark terror (sheer fear), vestiges of fear (small traces), residual doubt (doubt that remains).
Think as you read: the 'misadventure' is being thrown into the deep end; he planned to spring up from the bottom; the experience left him with a fear of water for years.
Extract-based MCQs often ask about the meaning of a phrase, the narrator's feeling, or a device in the drowning scene.

example.q: Extract (paraphrased): He thrashed wildly at the surface, gulped water and choked; his legs would not rise and dangled, heavy and frozen. Identify the feeling.
steps: Thrashing wildly (the text's word is 'flailed') shows helpless movement.
Choking and frozen legs show physical failure.
Together they convey panic.
example.answer: Panic and helplessness.

learn.reallife: Sports commentators use vivid sensory words, 'the ball skids, the crowd roars', to make you feel a match. Douglas does the same for drowning.

A long answer can link Douglas's lesson to the student's own life.
Discussion questions invite personal fears overcome.

The near-death experience made him value life more.
His will to live grew stronger.

topics.title: The peddler and his big idea

learn.hook: A poor man selling wire traps decides the whole world is one giant trap. Is he bitter, or is he on to something?
points: Author: Selma Lagerlöf, a Swedish writer and the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature (1909).
Setting: the iron-mining area of Värmland in Sweden, with its forges, mines and forests.
The peddler sells small rattraps of wire; his trade earns too little, so he begs and steals now and then to keep body and soul together.
His big idea: the world is a rattrap. Its riches and joys, shelter and food, heat and clothing are baits, and whoever touches them is caught.
He takes a bitter pleasure in this idea, amused at people who fall into the trap.

example.q: Explain the peddler's 'rattrap' philosophy in your own words.
steps: A rattrap offers cheese or meat as bait.
The world offers wealth, comfort and joy as bait.
People who grab them lose their freedom, like rats in a trap.
example.answer: The world tempts people with material things, and those who reach for them get trapped by greed.

learn.reallife: Online 'easy money' scams and lucky-draw tricks in India work exactly like the peddler's rattrap: a tempting bait, then a trap.

quiz.explain: It amused him to think of people who were caught.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the idea brought him practical gain

quiz.explain: Both true; R explains what he meant by A.

options: Language is the key to a people's freedom

quiz.explain: The car is bait, and the debt is the trap.
quiz.mistake: Picks a theme from another chapter

topics.title: The lonely crofter and the thirty kronor

learn.hook: A lonely old man is so glad of company that he shows a stranger exactly where he keeps his money.
points: One evening the peddler is welcomed into a little grey cottage by an old crofter who lives alone with no wife or child.
The crofter gives him porridge for supper, a big slice of tobacco, and plays mjölis, a card game, with him till bedtime.
He proudly says his cow's milk earned him thirty kronor last month, and shows the three ten-kronor notes kept in a leather pouch on a nail in the window frame.
Next morning the peddler comes back, smashes a pane, steals the money and hangs the pouch back. To avoid capture he takes a forest road, gets lost and realises he too is caught in a rattrap.
The crofter: lonely, generous and trusting.

example.q: How does the peddler realise he is caught in a rattrap?
steps: He took the bait: the thirty kronor.
Now he is lost in a big, dark forest, unable to find his way out.
Like a rat, he has been tempted and trapped.
example.answer: After stealing the bait (the money), he is lost in the forest and sees that he himself is trapped.

learn.reallife: Police in India often warn senior citizens living alone not to show cash or share bank details with strangers; loneliness can make trust risky.

topics.title: A case of mistaken identity at Ramsjö

learn.hook: Lost, cold and hungry, the peddler wanders into a forge, and the ironmaster greets him as an old army friend.
points: Lost in the forest, the peddler reaches the Ramsjö ironworks and is allowed to warm himself in the forge.
The ironmaster, on his night round, mistakes him for an old regimental comrade, Captain von Stahle, and invites him home for Christmas. The peddler does not correct him.
He declines, fearing that going to the manor house with stolen money would be like walking into the lion's den.
The ironmaster's daughter, Edla Willmansson, comes and persuades him with kindness to come.

Next morning, after he has been bathed, shaved and dressed, the ironmaster sees in daylight he is not the captain and wants to throw him out; he even threatens the sheriff. The ironmaster is impulsive and proud.

example.q: Why did the peddler first refuse the ironmaster's invitation?
steps: He had stolen thirty kronor and still had it.
A grand house full of people meant more risk of discovery.
He compared it to throwing himself into the lion's den.
example.answer: He feared being found out with the stolen money; going to the manor felt like walking into the lion's den.

learn.reallife: Indian cinema loves mistaken identity, from twin brothers to look-alikes. Lagerlöf uses the same device, but to test human goodness.

games.title: Who said or did it?

topics.title: Edla's kindness and the Christmas gift

learn.hook: Treat a man like a captain and he may start behaving like one. Edla's kindness proves it.
points: When her father wants to throw him out, Edla insists he stay: they had promised him Christmas cheer, and he should have one day of peace.
He spends Christmas Eve with the family and is treated with kindness and respect.
On Christmas morning, while the family is at church, he leaves. He leaves a small package for Edla: a rattrap holding the crofter's three ten-kronor notes and a letter.
In the letter he asks her to return the money to the old crofter, says he would have been caught in the world's rattrap had he not been treated like a captain, and signs it 'Captain von Stahle'.
The peddler: poor and bitter but redeemed by kindness. Edla: compassionate and mature; her goodness transforms him.

example.q: Why does the peddler sign the letter as 'Captain von Stahle'?
steps: Edla had treated him with the respect due to a captain.
That respect awakened his self-respect and goodness.
Signing as the captain shows he wants to live up to that respect.
example.answer: Edla's respect raised him to the dignity of a captain; signing so shows his moral change.

learn.reallife: Many Indian NGOs that work with former offenders say the same thing: respect and a fresh chance often change lives faster than punishment.

topics.title: Themes, metaphor and symbols

learn.hook: A rattrap catches rats. In this story, the same rattrap ends up setting a man free.
points: Theme 1: the world as a rattrap. Greed and temptation trap people, as they trap the peddler.
Theme 2: human goodness and the power of kindness to redeem; Edla's trust makes the peddler honest.
Theme 3: loneliness and the need for company, seen in the crofter and in the peddler's own life.
Devices: an extended metaphor of the rattrap; irony (a man is mistaken for a captain and then acts like one); gentle humour.
Symbols: the rattrap as temptation; the rattrap returned with the money as a Christmas gift symbolises his escape from the trap and his redemption.

example.q: Why is the peddler's Christmas gift ironic?
steps: The rattrap stood for his bitter view that the world traps people.
Now he uses a rattrap to return stolen money.
The symbol of being trapped becomes a symbol of his release.
example.answer: The rattrap, once his symbol of the world's cruelty, becomes the vehicle of his honesty and freedom.

learn.reallife: Festivals like Diwali and Eid are times of sharing. Lagerlöf sets her story at Christmas, the season of goodwill, to make the redemption feel natural.

topics.title: Words from the ironworks and reflexive pronouns

learn.hook: Trudge, plod, stumble: English has a dozen ways to say 'walk wearily'. The peddler uses most of them.
points: Phrases: 'keep body and soul together' (just survive), 'plods along' (walks slowly and heavily), 'unwonted joy' (unusual happiness), 'nodded a haughty consent' (agreed proudly), 'fallen into a line of thought' (begun thinking along one track).
Labels for the peddler: vagabond, stranger, tramp, ragamuffin (person in ragged clothes), guest.
Weary movement: lurch (sudden unsteady movement), stumble (trip), slog (work hard and long), trudge and plod (walk slowly and heavily).
Ironworks terms: hammer strokes, pig iron (crude iron from a furnace), coal dust, anvil (iron block on which metal is hammered).
Reflexive pronouns (myself, himself, themselves) refer back to the subject: 'He found himself caught.' Used for emphasis: 'The ironmaster himself came.'

example.q: Identify the use of 'himself' in: (a) The peddler saw himself in a trap. (b) The ironmaster himself opened the door.
steps: In (a), 'himself' is the object and refers to the subject (the peddler).
In (b), 'himself' only stresses who did it; removing it keeps the sentence complete.
So (a) is reflexive, (b) is emphatic.
example.answer: (a) reflexive use; (b) emphatic use.

learn.reallife: Indian steel plants at Bhilai or Jamshedpur still use terms like pig iron, ladle and anvil, words that would make sense to the forge workers of Ramsjö.

quiz.q: Which word does NOT describe weary movement?

quiz.q: Choose the correct sentence.

quiz.explain: The reflexive form for 'he' is 'himself'; 'hisself' is non-standard.

topics.title: Board exam practice: The Rattrap

learn.hook: Ironmaster vs Edla is a favourite board question. Know the contrast and you have the answer.
points: Think as you read: the rattrap idea came while thinking about his own traps; he was amused because people are caught; the crofter was talkative because he was lonely; he declined the invitation out of fear and accepted because of Edla's kindness.
How the peddler read kindness: at first he thought the crofter foolish and the ironmaster easy to fool; Edla's genuine kindness finally changed him.
Ironmaster vs Edla: he is impulsive, proud and quick to judge; she is observant, compassionate and generous.
Discussion: is the world a rattrap? how does loneliness affect people?

learn.reallife: The idea of reform through compassion appears in India's open jails, like Sanganer in Rajasthan, where trust is given to change behaviour.

topics.title: Fischer, Champaran and a persistent peasant

learn.hook: A poor, unlettered farmer follows Gandhi from city to city until he agrees to come. That stubbornness changed Indian history.
points: Author: Louis Fischer, an American journalist. 'Indigo' is an extract from his book 'The Life of Mahatma Gandhi'.
Fischer heard the story from Gandhi himself when he visited Gandhi's ashram at Sevagram in 1942.
Subject: Gandhi's Champaran movement of 1917 in Bihar for the indigo sharecroppers.
Rajkumar Shukla, a poor sharecropper from Champaran, met Gandhi at the annual Congress session at Lucknow in December 1916 and begged him to come.
Shukla was resolute: he followed Gandhi to Cawnpore and to his ashram near Ahmedabad until Gandhi named a date and asked him to meet him in Calcutta.

example.q: What quality of Rajkumar Shukla made the Champaran movement possible?
steps: Gandhi was busy and kept putting him off.
Shukla followed him from Lucknow to Cawnpore to Ahmedabad.
His persistence finally won Gandhi's promise.
example.answer: His persistence and determination; he did not give up until Gandhi agreed to come.

learn.reallife: Ordinary citizens still move change in India through persistence: from RTI petitions to repeated letters that finally get a village road built.

topics.title: The road to Champaran and the tinkathia system

learn.hook: Three parts in twenty: that tiny fraction of land kept thousands of families in misery for years.
points: From Calcutta they went to Patna. At Rajendra Prasad's house (he was away), the servants took Gandhi for another poor peasant and would not let him draw water from the well, fearing he was an untouchable.
At Muzaffarpur, Professor J.B. Kripalani received him at the station at midnight with students; lawyers came to meet him too.
Tinkathia system: Champaran's sharecroppers were bound by contract to grow indigo on 15 per cent (3 parts in 20) of their land and give the whole crop to the British landlords as rent.
When Germany developed synthetic indigo, the indigo crop lost its value. Landlords then got the peasants to sign agreements to pay compensation for being released from the 15 per cent arrangement.

Gandhi met the secretary of the British landlords' association, who refused information to an 'outsider', and the British commissioner of the Tirhut division, who bullied him and told him to leave Tirhut.

example.q: Why was the landlords' demand for compensation unfair?
steps: Synthetic indigo had made the crop worthless to the landlords anyway.
They still made the peasants pay to be released from growing it.
So they profited twice from the peasants' ignorance.
example.answer: Indigo was no longer valuable, yet landlords made peasants pay compensation to end an obligation that had lost its worth.

learn.reallife: Exploitative contracts with poor farmers are not just history. India's debates on contract farming still ask how to protect sharecroppers from unfair terms.

topics.title: Motihari: the first civil disobedience

learn.hook: An order says 'Leave'. A man writes back, politely, 'I will not.' Thousands of peasants arrive to watch what happens next.
points: Gandhi went to Motihari, the capital of Champaran. On his way to see a maltreated peasant, he was stopped and served an official notice to quit Champaran immediately.
He signed the receipt and wrote on it that he would disobey the order. He was summoned to court the next day.
In court he pleaded guilty, saying he had disobeyed not out of disrespect for the law but in obedience to the 'higher law of our being, the voice of conscience'.
Thousands of peasants gathered spontaneously at the court; the officials felt powerless. Gandhi helped them control the crowd.
Some days later the case was dropped on the orders of the Lieutenant-Governor. Civil disobedience had triumphed for the first time in modern India.

example.q: What does 'the higher law of our being, the voice of conscience' mean?
steps: Ordinary law is made by rulers.
Conscience is a person's inner sense of right and wrong.
When the two clash, Gandhi obeys conscience and accepts the penalty.
example.answer: Gandhi placed his moral sense of right above an unjust official order, and was willing to bear the punishment.

learn.reallife: Peaceful protest is part of India's democratic heritage. Civil disobedience means breaking an unjust law openly and accepting the penalty, not violence.

topics.title: The 25 per cent settlement

learn.hook: Why would a leader accept only half of what he asked? Because the real prize was not money.
points: An official commission of inquiry was set up; Gandhi was the sole representative of the peasants. Evidence went against the planters, and they agreed in principle to refund money to the peasants.
Gandhi asked for 50 per cent. The planters' spokesman offered 25 per cent, and Gandhi accepted, breaking the deadlock.
His reason: the amount was less important than the fact that the landlords had been forced to surrender part of the money and, with it, part of their prestige.
The peasants learnt that they had rights and defenders. Within a few years the British planters abandoned their estates, which went back to the peasants; indigo sharecropping disappeared.

example.q: Why did Gandhi accept a 25 per cent refund?
steps: He had asked for 50; the planters offered 25.
What mattered was that the landlords had to give back money at all.
That broke their prestige and showed peasants they had rights.
example.answer: Because the act of refunding broke the landlords' prestige and gave peasants courage; the amount was secondary.

learn.reallife: In negotiations, from wage talks to cricket board disputes, winning the principle often matters more than the exact amount. Gandhi knew this in 1917.

topics.title: Beyond politics: schools, health and self-reliance

learn.hook: Most leaders would leave after winning. Gandhi stayed on to open schools and teach villagers to keep clean.
points: Gandhi saw the deeper problems of cultural and social backwardness and opened primary schools in six villages.
Teachers included his disciples Mahadev Desai and Narhari Parikh with their wives, his youngest son Devdas, and his wife Kasturba.
Kasturba taught personal cleanliness and community sanitation. A doctor volunteered for six months with three medicines: castor oil, quinine and sulphur ointment.
Gandhi refused the help of C.F. Andrews, an English follower, because relying on an Englishman would show weakness; Indians had to rely on themselves.
Self-reliance and courage: the Champaran movement taught Indians to stand on their own feet.

example.q: Why did Gandhi refuse to let C.F. Andrews stay in Champaran?
steps: The lawyers wanted an Englishman on their side in an unequal fight.
Gandhi said this showed the weakness of their hearts.
The cause was just, so they had to rely on themselves.
example.answer: Depending on an Englishman would show weakness; Gandhi wanted Indians to be self-reliant.

learn.reallife: Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, launched in 2014 on Gandhi's birth anniversary, echoes what Kasturba taught in Champaran: sanitation is part of freedom.

topics.title: Themes: non-violence, rights and freedom from fear

learn.hook: 'The British could not order me about in my own country.' Gandhi called this a very ordinary thing. It was revolutionary.
points: Civil disobedience and non-violence: Gandhi broke an unjust order openly and peacefully, and accepted the penalty.
Peasants' rights: for the first time the peasants saw that they could stand up to the planters and win.
Freedom from fear: Gandhi told the lawyers that relief lay in freeing the peasants from fear, not in law courts.
Civil disobedience today: peaceful, lawful protest is part of democracy; it differs from violence or vandalism, and it means accepting legal consequences.

example.answer: Courts drained their money; what they needed was freedom from fear.

learn.reallife: The Constitution of India protects the right to assemble peacefully and without arms (Article 19(1)(b)); non-violence remains the core of lawful protest.

topics.title: Board exam practice: Indigo

learn.hook: 'Why is Champaran called a turning point in Gandhi's life?' This question appears again and again. Here is how to nail it.
points: Shukla's persistence: he followed Gandhi from Lucknow to Cawnpore to Ahmedabad.
The 25 per cent refund: the principle and the surrender of prestige mattered more than the amount.
Impact on peasants: courage, rights, the end of indigo sharecropping; schools and sanitation in villages.
Turning point: Gandhi said it was the moment he decided the British could not order him about in his own country; it began freedom from fear for ordinary Indians.

Short answer on tinkathia: 15 per cent (3/20) of land under indigo, given as rent; compensation demanded after German synthetic indigo. Long answer on self-reliance: the Andrews episode, schools, sanitation.

example.q: Write a 50-word answer: Why did Gandhi consider Champaran a turning point?
steps: Point: he defied British authority openly for the first time in India.
Detail: refused to leave, pleaded guilty, case dropped.
Significance: showed Indians could win by non-violence, free of fear.
example.answer: At Champaran Gandhi first declared that the British could not order him about in his own country. His successful civil disobedience freed peasants from fear and proved that non-violent resistance could win, shaping the whole freedom struggle.

learn.reallife: Champaran's centenary was marked in 2017 across Bihar, a reminder that a district's fight for fair farming grew into a national movement.

topics.title: Gemini Studios and the make-up room

learn.hook: Make-up bought by the truckload, a room once said to be a British general's stables, and lights hot enough to fry an actor. Welcome to Gemini Studios.
points: Author: Asokamitran, a Tamil writer who worked at Gemini Studios, Madras, from 1952 to the mid-1960s. The chapter is an extract from his memoir 'My Years with Boss'.
Tone: a humorous memoir. 'The Boss' is S.S. Vasan, the founder of Gemini Studios.
Pancake: the brand of make-up material that Gemini Studios bought by the truckload for its actors.
The make-up department was upstairs in a building said to have been Robert Clive's stables.
Incandescent lights and large mirrors made it like a hair-cutting salon turned torture chamber; the heavy make-up turned decent-looking actors into crimson-hued monsters.

example.q: Explain the title 'Poets and Pancakes'.
steps: 'Pancakes' refers to Pancake, the make-up brand used at Gemini.
'Poets' refers to the many poets and writers who worked there, like Subbu.
Together they sum up the studio: glamour and literature side by side.
example.answer: Pancake is the make-up brand; poets are the studio's writers. The title captures the two worlds of Gemini Studios.

learn.reallife: Today's film sets in Hyderabad's Ramoji Film City or Mumbai's Film City still have make-up vans and hot lights, but cooler LED lighting has made the 'torture chamber' far gentler.

topics.title: National integration and the frustrated office boy

learn.hook: A Bengali, a Maharashtrian, a Kannadiga, an Andhra, an Anglo-Burmese and local Tamils, all in one make-up room. The author calls it 'national integration', with a wink.
points: The make-up department showed 'national integration': a Bengali chief (later succeeded by a Maharashtrian), with a Dharwar Kannadiga, an Andhra, a Madras Indian Christian, an Anglo-Burmese and local Tamils.
Strict hierarchy: the chief made up the main actors, his assistants the lesser players, and the office boy the crowd players.
The office boy, in his early forties, had joined the studio hoping to become a star actor, screenwriter, director or lyricist. He was a bit of a poet, but stayed in a dead-end job.
Frustrated, he blamed Kothamangalam Subbu, the No. 2 at Gemini, for his failure and poured out his anger to the author.

example.q: How does the author create humour with the phrase 'national integration'?
steps: National integration is a grand political ideal.
He applies it to a small, noisy make-up room.
The mismatch between the big phrase and the small setting is funny.
example.answer: By using a serious national ideal to describe a mixed group of make-up men; the mock-grand phrase is humorous.

learn.reallife: Indian film crews today still bring together people from every state. A single Bollywood or Tollywood set may hear five languages before lunch.

topics.title: Subbu the genius and 'the opposition'

learn.hook: One man is cheerful, loyal and endlessly creative. Another, nicknamed 'the opposition', ends a career with a tape recorder.
points: Kothamangalam Subbu: the No. 2 at Gemini, a poet and the Boss's loyal aide; always cheerful, and able to suggest many ways of shooting a scene.
He wrote poetry and the novel 'Thillana Mohanambal', acted well, and supported many dependants with great generosity.
The legal adviser, nicknamed 'the opposition' by others, was the only one in pants, tie and sometimes a coat, while others wore khadi.
He once secretly recorded an actress's angry outburst on the set and played it back to her; she was stunned into silence, and her career ended.

example.q: Why was the legal adviser called 'the opposition'?
steps: A legal adviser should help the studio.
Instead, his actions, like taping the actress, harmed the studio's work.
So, ironically, he worked like the opposition.
example.answer: Because instead of helping, he often created problems, as when he ended a talented actress's career.

learn.reallife: Many Indian film studios have had creative all-rounders like Subbu: writer, lyricist and actor in one. Tamil cinema still celebrates such multi-talented artists.

topics.title: Clippings, a closed department and the MRA visit

learn.hook: The author's job was cutting newspapers. Everyone thought he did nothing. Then two hundred foreigners arrived to stage plays.
points: The author's job was to cut out newspaper clippings on many subjects and file them. Because he sat in a cubicle with scissors and paper, others thought he did nothing.
The Story Department of writers and poets was eventually closed, and the legal adviser, part of it, lost his job too.
Gemini Studios was anti-communist; most of its people wore khadi and admired Gandhi. The Boss welcomed the Moral Re-Armament Army (MRA), an international anti-communist group, in 1952.
About two hundred MRA members staged the plays 'Jotham Valley' and 'The Forgotten Factor'. Tamil drama later copied their sunrise and sunset scenes.

example.q: Why did people think the author did nothing?
steps: His work was quiet: cutting and filing newspapers.

example.answer: His quiet job of cutting newspaper clippings looked to others like idleness, so they came to him to pour out their troubles.

learn.reallife: Research teams in Indian newsrooms still keep 'clippings libraries'. What looked like 'nothing' to Gemini staff is the backbone of good research.

topics.title: The mystery poet: Stephen Spender

learn.hook: An English poet gives a long speech to a Tamil film studio. Nobody understands a word, and nobody knows who he is.
points: An English poet visited Gemini Studios and spoke to the staff. His accent and subject were beyond them; nobody understood him, and why he had come remained a mystery.
Years later the author found out: the visitor was Stephen Spender, the English poet and editor of the magazine 'The Encounter'.
Spender was one of the contributors to 'The God That Failed', essays by former communists: André Gide, Richard Wright, Ignazio Silone, Arthur Koestler, Louis Fischer and Spender himself.
The episode shows the cultural gap between an English poet and Tamil film workers, and the anti-communist mood of the era.

example.q: Why was the poet's visit a 'mystery'?

example.answer: His speech made no sense to the audience, and his purpose at a Tamil film studio was never clear.

learn.reallife: International writers still visit Indian festivals like the Jaipur Literature Festival. Today, translators and subtitles help bridge the gap that left Gemini's staff baffled.

topics.title: How Asokamitran makes us laugh

learn.hook: Asokamitran never tells a joke. He just describes things with a straight face, and that is what makes them funny.
points: Humour, irony and gentle satire on the film industry: hot lights that make actors into monsters, a 'national integration' of make-up men.
Self-deprecating humour: the author laughs at himself, calling his job one that others thought was doing nothing.
Irony and understatement: the legal adviser called 'the opposition'; a lawyer losing his job because poets were sent home.
Mock-heroic description: small matters told in grand language, such as Clive's stables or national integration.
Anecdotal structure: the chapter is a chain of anecdotes; characters like the office boy, Subbu and the legal adviser are drawn almost as caricatures.

example.q: Identify the device: 'The make-up department was said to have been Robert Clive's stables.'
steps: A great historical name is attached to a humble room.

example.answer: Mock-heroic irony: a lofty historical reference used for an ordinary make-up room.

learn.reallife: Indian comic writers like R.K. Laxman, in his cartoons, used the same straight-faced irony to poke fun at offices and officials.

topics.title: Board exam practice: Poets and Pancakes

learn.hook: Subbu, the MRA and Spender: three short-answer favourites. One long answer on humour. Let's lock them in.
points: Think as you read: Pancake is the make-up brand; the office boy was a frustrated would-be star; the author was thought to do nothing because he cut newspapers.
Understanding: humour through irony, exaggeration and self-mockery; Subbu as a many-sided genius (poet, novelist, actor, generous friend); the legal adviser who ended an actress's career.
The poet's visit was a mystery because no one understood him; 'The God That Failed' was a book of essays by ex-communists, including Spender.
Discussion: humour as a tool to criticise gently; the place of poetry and lyrics in Indian films.
Long answer on humour: give at least three examples, such as Clive's stables, 'national integration', the 'opposition' nickname and the do-nothing author.

topics.title: The interview: an art or an intrusion?

learn.hook: Every evening, news channels run interviews with cricketers, ministers and film stars. Yet until the mid-1800s, the interview did not even exist as a form of journalism.
points: Part I: Christopher Silvester's introduction to 'The Penguin Book of Interviews', on the history of interviews and views about them.
Part II: an extract from Mukund Padmanabhan's interview with the Italian writer Umberto Eco, published in The Hindu.
The interview was invented a little over 130 years before Silvester wrote, and has become a commonplace of journalism.
Positive view: at its best the interview is a source of truth and, in practice, an art; the interviewer holds great power and influence.
Negative view: an unwarranted intrusion into private lives that diminishes the celebrities interviewed.

example.q: Why is the interview described as a 'commonplace of journalism'?
steps: Commonplace means ordinary and very common.
Today interviews appear daily in newspapers, TV and online.
So, though it was invented only about 130 years earlier, it is now everywhere.
example.answer: Because interviews have become so common in the media that almost everyone has read or seen one.

learn.reallife: From post-match interviews at the IPL to budget-day interviews with the Finance Minister, the interview is a routine part of Indian media today.

topics.title: Writers who dreaded interviewers

learn.hook: One of the world's most loved children's writers refused every interviewer who knocked. He had his reasons.
points: Some primitive cultures believe a photograph steals a person's soul; similarly, V.S. Naipaul felt that some people are wounded by interviews and lose a part of themselves.
Lewis Carroll, author of 'Alice in Wonderland', had a 'defensive dread' of interviewers and never consented to be interviewed; he hated being lionised.
Rudyard Kipling called the interview immoral, a crime, an offence against his person, an assault that deserved punishment, and cowardly and vile.
Kipling's wife wrote in her diary that their day was 'wrecked by two reporters from Boston'.

example.q: What is the link between the 'photograph steals the soul' belief and Naipaul's view?
steps: The belief: a camera takes away part of a person's spirit.
Naipaul: an interview takes away part of the person interviewed.
Both see a loss of self in being recorded.
example.answer: Both suggest that being photographed or interviewed takes away a part of a person's self.

learn.reallife: Some Indian sportspeople avoid media before big events. Like Carroll, they feel constant attention takes something away from them.

topics.title: Who is Umberto Eco?

learn.hook: A professor of 'signs' writes a medieval murder mystery that sells millions of copies. Meet Umberto Eco.
points: Umberto Eco: an Italian professor of semiotics, the study of signs and symbols, at the University of Bologna.
His work spans scholarly books on semiotics, literary interpretation and medieval aesthetics, plus essays and novels.
His novel 'The Name of the Rose' (1980), a medieval detective story, sold between 10 and 15 million copies.
He calls himself a university professor who writes novels on Sundays: he sees himself first as an academic.

Novels are something he does in his spare time.

example.answer: He sees himself mainly as a scholar; novel-writing is a weekend or spare-time pursuit.

learn.reallife: Many Indian professionals write novels on the side: doctors, IAS officers and bankers. Like Eco, their 'Sunday' writing sometimes becomes a bestseller.

topics.title: Interstices and a playful style

learn.hook: How does one man write scholarly books, essays, a newspaper column and bestselling novels? He uses the gaps.
points: Eco works in 'interstices', the small empty spaces of time between tasks, such as waiting for a lift to arrive.
He says that if all the empty space were removed from the universe's atoms, the universe would be as small as his fist; likewise, our lives are full of empty spaces we can use.
His scholarly writing uses a playful, personal, narrative style, telling the story of his research instead of being dry and formal.
Theme: creativity and the efficient use of time.
Metaphor: 'interstices', literally tiny gaps between things, is used for the small gaps in a day.

example.q: Give an example of using 'interstices' in a student's day.
steps: Find a small gap: the 10-minute bus ride to school.
Use it for a small task: revising formula cards or new words.
Many such gaps add up to hours of work.
example.answer: Revising flashcards during a short bus ride or while waiting for class is using interstices.

learn.reallife: Students revising on the Mumbai local or the Delhi Metro are using Eco's interstices. Ten minutes twice a day adds up to over 100 hours in a year.

topics.title: Why did The Name of the Rose succeed?

learn.hook: A difficult novel full of medieval history and theology became a global bestseller. Even its author called this a mystery.
points: Eco thinks the novel's success is a mystery; he says it might not have sold if written ten years earlier or ten years later.
The novel is serious and demanding, a detective story that goes into metaphysics, theology and medieval history, yet it found a mass audience.
Eco suggests readers do not only want easy reading; many enjoy serious, challenging books, and the medieval setting attracted them.
Theme: popularity, scholarship and fiction can meet; a scholar can be a bestselling novelist.
Form: Part I is expository prose packed with quotations; Part II follows a question-answer interview format.

Readers were drawn by its medieval setting and serious content.

learn.reallife: Indian bestsellers on mythology and history show the same thing Eco noticed: readers will take on serious, layered stories when the setting fascinates them.

topics.title: Understanding the text: The Interview

learn.hook: 'Who is lionised today?' Answer that, and you'll see why writers like Carroll ran from reporters.
points: Positive views: art, source of truth, a way to know contemporaries. Negative views: intrusion, diminishing, wounding, a crime. Celebrity writers dislike interviews because they intrude and take something away.
The photograph belief: primitive cultures fear a picture steals the soul; 'thumbprints on his windpipe' means a choking, suffocating feeling.
To be lionised is to be treated as a celebrity. Today film stars, sports stars and influencers are lionised because of media attention.
Eco's interstices explain his output; his academic writing is personal and playful because he tells research as a story.
Eco on his novel's success: a mystery of timing; readers liked its serious content and medieval setting.

example.q: Who is lionised today, and why?
steps: Lionise = treat as a celebrity.
Examples: cricketers, film stars, social media influencers.
Reason: constant media coverage and public admiration.

learn.reallife: When an Indian athlete wins Olympic gold, crowds, interviews and ads follow within hours. That is lionising, and Carroll's 'horror' of it makes more sense.

topics.title: Conducting an interview and exam answers

learn.hook: Your school magazine wants an interview with the principal. You have 15 minutes. What do you ask?
points: The interview as journalism: it informs, reveals personality and shapes opinion, but must respect privacy and consent.
Planning an interview: research the person, prepare open questions (what, why, how), start easy, then go deeper, and listen and follow up.
Conducting it: take permission to record, be polite, note exact words, check facts before publishing.
Short answers: views on interviews (positive and negative) and Eco's interstices. Long answer: the interview as a medium, its power, art and risks.

example.answer: What made you choose medicine? What is a typical day like at your clinic? What advice would you give students who want to become doctors?

learn.reallife: Podcasts by Indian entrepreneurs and sportspeople show interviews at their best: well-researched questions, real listening and respect for the guest.

topics.title: Sophie's big dreams, Jansie's hard facts

learn.hook: Two school-leavers walk home. One plans a boutique and a film career; the other knows the biscuit factory is waiting.
points: Author: A.R. Barton. 'Going Places' is a story of adolescent fantasy set in a working-class English family.
Narration: third person, but it closely follows Sophie's thoughts and daydreams.
Sophie and her friend Jansie are about to leave school. Jansie says they are both 'earmarked for the biscuit factory'.
Sophie dreams of opening a boutique, becoming an actress or a fashion designer, anything glamorous.
Jansie is practical: she reminds Sophie that a boutique needs money and that such jobs need experience.

steps: Sophie imagines a boutique, acting or fashion design.
Jansie expects work at the biscuit factory.

learn.reallife: Many Indian teens dream of being influencers or film stars while family finances point to a nearby job. Sophie's tug-of-war between dream and reality is very familiar.

Sophie admires Geoff, an apprentice mechanic who travels across the city to work and keeps his life private; she longs to be part of his world.
She tells Geoff she met Danny Casey, the young Irish football star of United, in the arcade.

topics.title: The match, the canal and the broken fantasy

learn.hook: At the match, Sophie's family cheers as Danny Casey scores. Later, Sophie waits alone by the canal. Nobody comes.
points: At the United match, Sophie stands with her father and little Derek (Geoff is with his mates); Danny Casey scores a goal, and Sophie feels a private thrill as if he were hers.
Later Sophie walks by the canal and waits on a bench under a solitary elm. Casey never comes.
She goes home sad, but she still clings to the fantasy; her worry is how to keep the truth from others, especially Geoff.
Contrast: dreamy Sophie against realistic Jansie; the canal meeting stands for illusion, a meeting that was never real.

example.q: What does the canal scene reveal about Sophie?
steps: She waits for a meeting that probably never existed.
When Casey does not come, she is sad but does not give up the dream.
This shows how deep her need for fantasy is.
example.answer: It reveals that she lives in illusion; even disappointment does not break her fantasy.

learn.reallife: Social media lets fans feel close to stars they have never met. Sophie's canal is an old-fashioned version of waiting for a reply to a fan message.

topics.title: Themes and the irony of the title

learn.hook: 'Going places' means heading for success. Sophie isn't going anywhere, and that is exactly the point.
points: Adolescent fantasy and hero worship: Sophie idolises Danny Casey and builds a fantasy around him.
Dreams versus reality, and the limits of class: a poor family's daughter is likely to work at a factory, whatever her dreams.
Communication gaps in the family: Geoff keeps to himself, the father dismisses her, the mother is too tired to listen.
Irony of the title: 'going places' means rising in life, but Sophie's prospects are limited; she goes nowhere except in her dreams.

example.answer: The title promises success, but Sophie's real prospects are limited; she travels only in fantasy.

learn.reallife: Hero worship of cricketers in India runs deep. Admiring heroes can inspire, but replacing real plans with fantasy can leave teens like Sophie stranded.

topics.title: Kamala Das and a drive to Cochin

learn.hook: A short car ride to the airport. A mother dozing in the seat beside you. In that ordinary moment, Kamala Das finds a lifetime of fear.
points: Poet: Kamala Das, an Indian poet who wrote in English and Malayalam (as Madhavikutty), known for frank, confessional poetry.
Form: a short autobiographical poem written as one long sentence, with no stanza breaks; the flow mirrors a rush of thoughts.
Situation: the poet drives from her parents' home to Cochin airport on a Friday morning.
Her mother sits beside her, dozing with her mouth open.

steps: The poem records one continuous stream of thought and feeling.
A single sentence shows feelings flowing without pause.
It matches the short car ride, from home to the airport.
example.answer: The single sentence mirrors an unbroken flow of thoughts and emotions during one journey.

learn.reallife: Many Indian students living away from home in Kota, Bengaluru or Delhi know the airport goodbye with a parent. This poem captures the feeling behind it.

topics.title: A face like a corpse, a mind that turns away

learn.hook: Sometimes you notice, all at once, that a parent has grown old. The poet's first instinct is to look away.
points: Looking at her sleeping mother, the poet sees her face ashen like a corpse's and realises with pain that her mother is as old as she looks.
She pushes the thought away and looks outside at young trees sprinting past and merry children spilling out of their homes.
At the airport, after the security check, she looks at her mother again: wan and pale as a late winter's moon.
An old childhood fear returns: the fear of losing her mother, felt now as a familiar ache.

example.q: Why does the poet look out of the window?
steps: The sight of her mother's ashen face is painful.
Outside, the trees and children are full of life.
Looking away helps her escape the thought of ageing and death.
example.answer: To escape the painful thought of her mother's ageing; the lively scene outside is a distraction.

learn.reallife: Many of us scroll our phones or change the subject when a hard thought comes up. The poet's glance out of the window is the same human reflex.

topics.title: 'See you soon, Amma': love that hides its fear

learn.hook: Three simple words: 'See you soon.' Behind them lies everything the poet cannot say.
points: At parting, the poet hides her feelings and says only, 'See you soon, Amma.'
She smiles and smiles and smiles, to reassure her mother and to hide her own fear.
Theme: the ageing of a parent and the fear of separation and death.
Theme: love, helplessness and suppressed emotion; she cannot stop time, so she covers her pain with hope.

example.q: What do the parting words 'See you soon, Amma' convey?
steps: They sound casual and cheerful.
In fact they express hope that her mother will live to meet her again.
They also hide the poet's fear.
example.answer: Hope of meeting again and an attempt to hide fear and reassure her mother.

learn.reallife: Indian families often keep goodbyes light, 'Phone kar dena, beta', even when they are worried. The poet's smile is that same brave lightness.

topics.title: Youth versus age: similes and images

learn.hook: Inside the car: an old woman asleep. Outside: trees racing and children bursting out of homes. Two worlds, one window apart.
points: Theme: the contrast between youth and old age, life and decay.
Similes: the face 'ashen like that of a corpse'; the mother 'pale as a late winter's moon'.
Imagery: young trees sprinting; merry children spilling out of their homes, full of energy and joy.
Personification: the trees are described as sprinting, as if they were runners; in a moving car they seem to race past.

example.q: Why are the trees said to be 'sprinting'?
steps: From a moving car, roadside trees seem to rush backwards.
'Sprinting' gives them life and speed, like young runners.
This energy contrasts with the dozing mother.
example.answer: From the moving car they seem to run past; the word gives them youthful energy that contrasts with the mother's age.

learn.reallife: Look out of a Vande Bharat window and the trees seem to race by. The poet uses that everyday effect to say something deep about time.

topics.title: Repetition, free verse and the poet's ache

learn.hook: 'Smile and smile and smile.' Say it aloud. Does it sound happy, or does it sound like someone trying very hard?
points: Repetition: 'smile and smile and smile' shows the effort of keeping up a brave face; the smile hides pain.
Structure: the contrast between inside the car (age) and outside (youth); enjambment, with lines running on; free verse, with no regular rhyme or metre.
The poet's pain is the realisation that her mother is old and may soon die; the ache is her childhood fear of losing her mother, now returning.
The trees are 'sprinting' because, from a moving car, they appear to rush backwards, and they stand for youth hurrying past.

example.q: What kind of pain and ache does the poet feel?
steps: Pain: realising her mother is truly old.
Ache: an old childhood fear of losing her.
Both come from love and the fear of separation by death.
example.answer: The pain of seeing her mother's age and the ache of her old fear of losing her for ever.

learn.reallife: Indian film songs often repeat a line to show feeling. Kamala Das's triple smile works the same way: the repetition is the emotion.

topics.title: Board exam practice: My Mother at Sixty-six

learn.hook: Extract-based questions on this poem almost always ask about a simile or the contrast. Let's practise.
points: Merry children: brought in to contrast youth and joy with the mother's old age and to distract the poet from her pain.
Late winter's moon: like the moon at the end of winter, the mother is pale, dim and near the end of her life.
Parting words and smile: hope of meeting again, and a brave mask over her fear.
Extract-based MCQs: identify similes ('ashen like', 'pale as'), the contrast between inside and outside, the poet's feelings; short answers on her fear.

example.q: Extract (paraphrased): after security, she looks at her mother again, pale like a late winter's moon, and feels the old ache. (a) Device? (b) Feeling?
steps: 'Pale as a late winter's moon' uses 'as': a simile.
The 'old familiar ache' is her childhood fear.
Feeling: fear of losing her mother.
example.answer: (a) Simile. (b) Fear and pain at the thought of losing her mother.

learn.reallife: CBSE extract questions reward precise terms. Writing 'simile' with the exact words, rather than 'comparison', can earn the full mark.

topics.title: Neruda's invitation: count to twelve

learn.hook: What if the whole planet stopped, just for a few seconds, at the same time? A Nobel-winning poet asks us to try.
points: Poet: Pablo Neruda, a Chilean poet and diplomat who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1971.
'Keeping Quiet' was written in Spanish and translated into English by Alastair Reid; it is in free verse.
Opening: the poet asks us to count to twelve and keep still, all over the earth, for once.
In that moment no one would speak in any language, and we would not move our arms.

example.q: Why does the poet want no one to speak 'in any language'?
steps: Languages can divide people into groups.
Silence is shared by everyone in the same way.
So a common silence unites all humanity.
example.answer: Because silence is universal; without language barriers, all people would share one moment together.

learn.reallife: India observes two minutes' silence on 30 January, Martyrs' Day. A whole nation pausing together is close to what Neruda imagines.

topics.title: A strange, exotic moment of peace

learn.hook: No engines. No rush. Fishermen sparing whales. Generals changing into clean clothes. Neruda paints a world on pause.
points: It would be an exotic moment, without rush and without engines; we would all be together in a sudden strangeness.
Fishermen in the cold sea would not harm whales.
The man gathering salt would look at his hurt hands, noticing his own pain for once.
Those who prepare green wars, wars with gas and fire, victories with no survivors, would put on clean clothes and walk with their brothers in the shade, doing nothing.

example.q: What does the image of the salt gatherer show?
steps: He works so hard that he never notices his injuries.
In the quiet moment he looks at his hurt hands.
Stillness lets people notice their own suffering.
example.answer: That constant work makes us ignore our pain; silence lets us see and care for ourselves.

learn.reallife: Workers in the salt pans of the Rann of Kutch, the Agariyas, are known to suffer injuries to their hands and feet from salt. Neruda's salt gatherer is real.

topics.title: Not death but life: the earth's lesson

learn.hook: Does Neruda want us to stop living? No. He wants us to stop rushing, which is very different.
points: The poet says he does not want total inactivity; life is what it is all about, and he wants nothing to do with death.
If we were not so single-minded about keeping our lives moving, a huge silence might end the sadness of never understanding ourselves and of threatening ourselves with death.
The earth can teach us: when everything seems dead in winter, it later proves to be alive in spring.
Ending: the poet counts to twelve, asks us to keep quiet, and leaves.

example.q: What lesson does the earth teach us?
steps: In winter, trees and fields seem dead.
In spring, life returns.
So stillness is not death; it can be a time of renewal.
example.answer: Apparent stillness can hold hidden life; like the earth, silence can renew us.

learn.reallife: A field after harvest in Punjab looks dead, but with the next sowing it is green again. Neruda's earth lesson is something every Indian farmer knows.

topics.title: Themes: silence, brotherhood and peace

learn.hook: Neruda's poem is short, but it touches war, ecology and the human mind all at once.
points: Silence and introspection: a pause lets us look within and understand ourselves.
Universal brotherhood, peace and non-violence: no language barriers; warmongers walking with their brothers.
Criticism of war, harm to nature and mindless activity: green wars, harming whales, endless rush.
Form: free verse and direct address to the reader with 'let us' and 'we', which includes everyone.

example.q: How does the poet promote universal brotherhood?
steps: Everyone keeps still at once, all over the earth.
No one speaks any language, removing barriers.
Former enemies walk together as brothers.
example.answer: By imagining all humanity sharing one silent moment, without language barriers or war, as brothers.

learn.reallife: Yoga and meditation, traditions with roots in India, now practised worldwide, value the same pause and introspection that Neruda praises.

topics.title: Devices and big questions

learn.hook: Repeated 'without', fishermen, whales, a salt gatherer: Neruda builds his message image by image.
points: Anaphora and repetition: lines starting the same way ('without rush, without engines') stress the absence of noise and haste.
Imagery: fishermen and whales, the salt gatherer, the warmongers; each shows a different harm we could pause.
Personification of the earth, which can 'teach' us; paradox of life hidden under apparent death.
Counting to twelve and keeping still would help us find peace, introspection and brotherhood. Twelve is often read as the hours on a clock face or the months of a year, a full cycle of time.
The poet does not advocate total inactivity or death: he says life is what it is all about.

example.q: Explain the paradox in the earth's lesson.
steps: A paradox seems self-contradictory but holds a truth.
Things that 'seem dead' are 'alive'.
Truth: rest and stillness hide life and renewal.
example.answer: It seems contradictory that dead things are alive, but in nature dormancy leads to new life; so silence can renew us.

learn.reallife: A neem tree sheds its leaves and stands bare, then bursts into fresh green leaves a few weeks later. That is the paradox of the earth that Neruda uses.

learn.hook: 'What sadness does the poet refer to?' is one of the most-asked short questions on this poem.

Symbol from nature: the earth, which seems dead but later proves to be alive, showing life under apparent stillness.
Lines that best convey the message: the call to count to twelve and keep still, and the line on life being what it is all about.

learn.reallife: Exam halls in India go silent before the paper starts. Many toppers say that minute of calm helps them think clearly, a small-scale 'Keeping Quiet'.
