topics.title: Keats and a joy that lasts for ever

learn.hook: A phone's wallpaper fades from your mind in a week. Keats claims some beautiful things never fade. Which ones, and why?
points: Poet: John Keats, an English Romantic poet. These lines are from the opening of his long poem 'Endymion'.
Form: rhyming couplets in iambic pentameter (heroic couplets): pairs of rhyming lines, each with five da-DUM beats.
Opening idea: a thing of beauty is a joy for ever; its loveliness keeps increasing and never passes into nothingness.
It keeps a quiet bower (a shady shelter) for us, and a sleep full of sweet dreams, health and quiet breathing.

example.q: What does Keats mean by 'a thing of beauty is a joy for ever'?
steps: Beautiful things give us joy.
That joy does not end; the memory of beauty stays with us.
In fact its loveliness grows each time we recall it.
example.answer: Beauty gives lasting joy; its memory never fades but grows stronger over time.

learn.reallife: Many people in India remember a first sight of the Himalayas or the Taj Mahal for decades. That lasting glow is exactly Keats's claim.

topics.title: A flowery band against the gloom

learn.hook: Life has bad days, bad people and bad news. Keats says we survive by tying ourselves to beauty, one flower at a time.
points: Every morning we weave a flowery band (wreath) that binds us to the earth: beautiful things keep us attached to life.
Beauty helps us in spite of despondence (despair), the inhuman dearth of noble natures (lack of good people), gloomy days and the unhealthy, darkened ways we follow.
Some shape of beauty moves away the pall (dark cloth covering a coffin, here sadness) from our dark spirits.

learn.reallife: On a bad day, a monsoon rainbow over Mumbai's Marine Drive or a chai-time sunset can lift the mood. Keats calls this beauty removing the pall.

topics.title: Keats's list of beautiful things

learn.hook: Sun, moon, sheep in shade, daffodils, cool streams, musk roses, heroic tales. Keats's list moves from nature to the human imagination.
points: Nature: the sun, the moon, trees old and young giving shade (a 'shady boon') to simple sheep, daffodils in their green world.
Clear rills (small streams) that make a cooling covert (shelter) against the hot season; the mid-forest brake (thicket) rich with musk-rose blooms.
Human imagination: the grandeur of the dooms (glorious fates) we imagine for the mighty dead, and all lovely tales we have heard or read.
Climax: an endless fountain of immortal drink pouring to us from heaven's brink, beauty as a divine gift.

learn.reallife: Tales of heroes like Rani Lakshmibai or Bhagat Singh still move Indian students. Keats counts such inspiring stories of the 'mighty dead' as things of beauty.

topics.title: Sound and style: alliteration, inversion and couplets

learn.hook: Read 'simple sheep' aloud. Feel the soft 's' sounds? Keats chose them on purpose.
points: Nature imagery throughout: sun, moon, trees, sheep, daffodils, rills, musk-roses.
Alliteration: repeated starting consonants, as in 'simple sheep' and 'noble natures'.
Inversion: normal word order reversed for rhythm, as in 'are we wreathing' instead of 'we are wreathing'.
Rhyming couplets and Romantic diction (o'er, 'gainst, boon, bower).

Exam lists: things of beauty (sun, moon, trees, sheep, daffodils, rills, musk-roses, tales, the mighty dead); things that cause suffering (despondence, dearth of noble natures, gloomy days, unhealthy ways).

example.q: Identify the device: 'Therefore, on every morrow, are we wreathing a flowery band'.
steps: Normal order would be 'we are wreathing'.
The verb comes before the subject here.
This reversal is inversion.
example.answer: Inversion (and a metaphor in 'flowery band').

learn.reallife: Bollywood lyricists often flip word order to fit a tune. Keats did the same to keep his couplets flowing.

topics.title: Understanding the poem: band, love of life and the mighty dead

learn.hook: Why do people love life even when it hurts? Keats's answer fits in one word: beauty.
points: 'Wreathing a flowery band to bind us to the earth' suggests that every day we gather beautiful experiences that keep us attached to life.
What makes humans love life despite troubles: some shape of beauty that removes the pall of sorrow from our spirits.
'Grandeur' is linked to the 'mighty dead' because great people of the past met glorious fates; imagining them inspires us and is a source of beauty.

example.q: What makes human beings love life in spite of troubles?
steps: Life has despondence, gloomy days and a lack of good people.
Yet some shape of beauty lifts the gloom.
So beauty keeps us attached to life.
example.answer: Beauty, in nature and in stories, lifts our sorrow and makes us love life despite troubles.

learn.reallife: Stories of the mighty dead, like the warriors and reformers in NCERT history, are things Indian students 'have heard or read' that inspire them.

topics.title: Board exam practice: A Thing of Beauty

learn.hook: Do beautiful things leave a lasting impression? Keats says yes, and the board exam wants you to prove it.
points: Lasting impression: yes. A thing of beauty is a joy for ever; its memory stays and its loveliness increases.
Image for the bounty of the earth: an endless fountain of immortal drink pouring from heaven's brink.
Extract-based MCQs ask about meaning, devices (metaphor, alliteration, inversion) and the theme of beauty.
Short answers on nature and beauty: link nature's healing power with Keats's claim that beauty is eternal.

example.q: Extract (paraphrased): beauty's loveliness increases and it will never pass into nothingness. (a) What does this tell us about beauty? (b) Find the opposite of 'nothingness' in the idea.
steps: (a) Beauty lasts and grows; it never dies.
(b) The idea opposes nothingness with 'joy for ever'.
So beauty is permanent.
example.answer: (a) Beauty is permanent and its charm increases. (b) Lasting joy, a 'joy for ever'.

learn.reallife: Photographers at Kaziranga or the Valley of Flowers say a single frame can stay with viewers for years, a modern proof of Keats's 'joy for ever'.

topics.title: Frost's little shed by the highway

learn.hook: On every Indian highway there are small stalls selling guavas, corn or jaggery, and most cars speed past. Robert Frost saw the same thing in America.
points: Poet: Robert Frost, an American poet known for poems about rural New England.
Type: a narrative-reflective poem on the plight of the rural poor living beside a busy highway.
Scene: a little old house with a new shed at the edge of the road, where the farmers sell produce to passers-by.
Their hope: a share of city money, so they can live a better life, the kind that city people and the movies promise.

example.q: What do the people who set up the stand want?
steps: They sell produce at the roadside.
They want some city money in their hands.
They hope it will let them live better, like city people.
example.answer: They want to earn some city money to improve their lives and enjoy the comforts city people have.

learn.reallife: Roadside stalls on the Mumbai–Pune expressway or NH-44 sell seasonal fruit. For many rural families, those small sales are a key source of cash.

topics.title: The polished traffic and its complaint

learn.hook: Shiny cars race past, their drivers thinking only of where they are going. If anyone looks at the stand, it is only to grumble.
points: The 'polished traffic' (rich city people in shiny cars) passes with its mind ahead, thinking only of its destination.
If anyone does glance aside, it is only to complain that the crudely painted signs, with N and S turned the wrong way, spoil the landscape.
Goods offered: wild berries in wooden quarts, crook-necked golden squash with silver warts, and even the beauty of the mountain scene.
The poet says the hurt to the scenery is not his complaint; his real complaint is the trusting sorrow of what is left unsaid.

example.q: Why does the city traffic complain?
steps: They notice the stand only for a moment.
They see clumsy signs with letters painted backwards.
They feel these spoil the pretty landscape.
example.answer: They complain that the badly painted signs, with N and S turned wrong, mar the beauty of the scenery.

learn.reallife: Travellers often post photos of 'spelling mistakes' on roadside boards. Frost would ask: did you also notice the family behind the board?

topics.title: Greedy good-doers and the squeal of brakes

learn.hook: News arrives that the rural folk will be 'helped': bought out and moved to villages near a theatre and a store. Frost is not impressed.
points: The poet hears that these 'pitiful kin' are to be bought out and gathered into villages near the theatre and the store, where they will not have to think for themselves.
'Greedy good-doers, beneficent beasts of prey' swarm over their lives, enforcing benefits meant to soothe them and teaching them to sleep all day, destroying their old way of sleeping at night.
The rural folk wait all day for the squeal of brakes. Cars stop only to turn round, to ask the way, or to ask for a gallon of gas.
In despair the poet sometimes wishes to put them out of their pain at once, then wonders, back in a saner mood, how he would feel if someone offered to do that to him.

example.q: Why does the poet change his mind about putting them out of their pain?
steps: At first, their endless disappointment seems unbearable.
Then he imagines someone doing the same to him.
He realises no one would want that; they deserve respect, not pity.
example.answer: Thinking how he himself would feel, he sees that their lives are precious and that such 'mercy' would be cruel.

learn.reallife: Development projects in India debate this very question: does moving rural people truly help them, or does it uproot them? Frost asks it in verse.

topics.title: Themes: poverty, hypocrisy and the poet's empathy

learn.hook: Frost is angry at three things at once: the rich who ignore, the planners who pretend, and his own helplessness.
points: Rural poverty and the indifference of the urban rich: the polished traffic ignores the stand.
Hypocrisy of welfare planners and agencies: 'greedy good-doers' who claim to help but exploit.
The poet's empathy and helplessness: he feels their pain but cannot change it.
Form: rhyming lines of varied length, giving a conversational, reflective flow.

example.q: How does the poet show empathy?
steps: He notices the unsaid sorrow behind the stand.
He can hardly bear their childish longing in vain.
He imagines himself in their place.
example.answer: By feeling their hidden sorrow, suffering with their disappointment, and imagining himself in their place.

learn.reallife: Programmes for farmer welfare in India work best when they listen to farmers. Frost's 'greedy good-doers' are a warning about the opposite.

topics.title: Devices and the city folk's attitude

learn.hook: 'Beneficent beasts of prey.' Two words that should not sit together, and that is the whole point.
points: Oxymoron: 'beneficent beasts of prey' joins kindness with predation to expose fake helpers. Alliteration: 'greedy good-doers', 'beneficent beasts'.
Irony and sarcasm: the 'help' that harms; the 'mercifully gathered in'. Imagery: the little stand, the polished traffic, the squeal of brakes.
City folk ignore the stand (the traffic passes with its mind ahead); if they look, it is only to complain about the badly painted signs that spoil the scene.
The plea of the rural folk: some city money in hand, to see if it will make their lives expand, the life the movies promise and the party in power is said to keep from them.

example.q: Identify the devices in 'greedy good-doers, beneficent beasts of prey'.
steps: 'Greedy good-doers': repeated 'g' sound, alliteration; 'greedy' with 'good' is also contradictory.
'Beneficent beasts': repeated 'b', alliteration.
'Beneficent' + 'beasts of prey': opposites joined, an oxymoron.
example.answer: Alliteration and oxymoron (with sarcasm).

learn.reallife: Indian political cartoons often use oxymorons like 'honest corruption'. Frost's phrase does the same job of exposing a contradiction.

topics.title: Board exam practice: A Roadside Stand

learn.hook: 'What is the childish longing, and why is it in vain?' Learn this answer and you're halfway through the extract questions.
points: Double standards of government and agencies: 'greedy good-doers', 'beneficent beasts of prey', 'enforcing benefits', 'soothe them out of their wits'.
Childish longing: the innocent hope that a passing car will stop and buy; it is in vain because cars stop only to turn round, ask the way or ask for gas.
The poet's pain: he can hardly bear the thought of so much childish longing in vain; the sadness lurks near the open window.
Extract MCQs: identify devices, the meaning of 'polished traffic' or 'mind ahead'; short answers on urban indifference and false welfare.

example.q: Write a 40-word answer: What is the 'childish longing' and why is it in vain?
steps: Define: the simple, innocent hope that cars will stop and buy.
Why in vain: cars stop only for their own needs.
Effect: the hope is never fulfilled.
example.answer: The childish longing is the rural folk's innocent hope that a car will stop to buy their produce. It is in vain, because cars stop only to turn round, ask the way or ask for a gallon of gas.

learn.reallife: Highway dhabas thrive when they meet travellers' needs; tiny stalls often struggle. Frost's poem gives a voice to the struggling stall.

topics.title: Adrienne Rich and the tigers on the screen

learn.hook: A quiet aunt sits stitching. On her cloth, bold yellow tigers leap through a green jungle. Why would a timid woman sew such fearless beasts?
points: Poet: Adrienne Rich, an American poet and feminist.
Form: three quatrains (four-line stanzas) in rhyming couplets, rhyme scheme aabb.
Aunt Jennifer's tigers prance across a screen, the embroidery panel she is stitching.
They are bright topaz denizens of a world of green: golden-yellow inhabitants of a green forest.

example.answer: The tigers are bright golden-yellow creatures who live naturally in the green jungle.

learn.reallife: Indian women's crafts like phulkari in Punjab or kantha in Bengal have long carried women's stories and dreams in thread, just like Aunt Jennifer's panel.

topics.title: Fearless tigers, fluttering fingers

learn.hook: The tigers pace like knights. Their maker can barely pull a needle. The contrast is the poem's heartbeat.
points: The tigers do not fear the men beneath the tree (hunters); they pace in sleek, chivalric certainty, confident and noble like knights.
Aunt Jennifer's fingers flutter through the wool; she finds even the light ivory needle hard to pull.
The massive weight of Uncle's wedding band sits heavily on her hand: marriage is a burden on her.

steps: An ivory needle is light.

example.answer: Because she is nervous and oppressed; the burden of her marriage makes even a light needle feel heavy.

learn.reallife: Studies on women's well-being show that stress and fear can show up in the body: shaky hands, tiredness. Rich captures this in 'fluttering fingers'.

topics.title: Ringed by ordeals, outlived by art

learn.hook: The aunt will die. The tigers will not. Rich ends the poem with art outliving its maker.
points: When Aunt Jennifer is dead, her terrified hands will still lie ringed with the ordeals she was mastered by: even death does not free her from her marriage's trials.
The tigers in the panel that she made will go on prancing, proud and unafraid.
Theme: art as escape and self-expression. Through her tigers she expresses the freedom and courage she lacks, and that art outlives the artist.

example.q: What is the meaning of 'ringed with ordeals she was mastered by'?
steps: 'Ringed' recalls the wedding ring.
'Ordeals' are her painful experiences in marriage.
'Mastered by' shows she was dominated and controlled.
example.answer: Her hands remain marked by the hardships of a marriage in which she was dominated, even after death.

learn.reallife: Paintings by Amrita Sher-Gil still speak powerfully decades after she died at 28. Art, as Rich says, goes on prancing after the artist is gone.

topics.title: Oppression, contrast, symbols and irony

learn.hook: A ring that weighs a ton, a needle that won't move, and tigers that never stop. Every image in this poem is a symbol.
points: Theme: the oppression of women in a patriarchal marriage; Uncle's wedding band dominates her life.
Contrast: fearless, confident tigers versus a timid, terrified aunt.
Symbols: tigers stand for freedom, courage and strength; the wedding band for bondage and male dominance; the ivory needle for the effort of a woman's self-expression.
Irony: a fearful woman creates fearless creatures; the art she makes has the freedom she never had.

example.q: Why is it ironic that Aunt Jennifer creates fearless tigers?
steps: She herself is terrified and dominated.
Her tigers are proud, free and unafraid.
She gives her art the qualities she lacks.
example.answer: Because a timid, oppressed woman makes creatures full of courage and freedom, qualities she can only express through art.

learn.reallife: India's laws on domestic violence (2005) and dowry (1961) aim to protect women. Rich's poem shows the quieter, emotional side of oppression.

topics.title: Charley and the station with three levels

learn.hook: Every official says New York's Grand Central Station has two levels. Charley insists there are three, because he has been to the third.
points: Author: Jack Finney, an American writer of science fiction and fantasy.
Narration: first person, by Charley; the story blends everyday realism with fantasy and time travel.
Charley, aged 31, insists that Grand Central Station in New York has three levels, though railway officials swear it has only two.
One night, working late and in a hurry to get home, he takes a short cut through the station, goes down some stairs and a corridor, gets lost, and finds himself on a third level.

example.q: Why does the story begin with railway officials denying a third level?
steps: It sets up a conflict between official fact and Charley's claim.
The reader is made curious: is he right or imagining?
This uncertainty runs through the whole story.
example.answer: It creates doubt and curiosity: the reader must decide whether Charley's third level is real or imagined.

learn.reallife: Big stations like Mumbai's CSMT or New Delhi have endless corridors and stairs. It is easy to imagine getting lost in one, and Finney uses that feeling.

learn.hook: Gas lamps, brass spittoons, derby hats and a steam engine with a funnel chimney. Charley has walked into the past.
points: The third level looks old: flickering gas lights, brass spittoons, people in old-fashioned clothes, derby hats, sideburns and fancy waistcoats, and an old locomotive like a Currier and Ives print.
He sees a newspaper, 'The World', dated 11 June 1894; the paper had not been published for years.
He tries to buy two tickets to Galesburg, Illinois, a peaceful town of that era, for himself and his wife Louisa.
The clerk looks at his modern money, says it is not money, and suspects him of trying to cheat. Charley hurries away.

topics.title: The first-day cover: proof from the past

learn.hook: An envelope postmarked 18 July 1894 turns up in a stamp album, with a letter from a man who vanished last week. The twist lands like a train.
points: Sam disappears. Later, in his grandfather's stamp collection, Charley finds a first-day cover postmarked 18 July 1894, with a letter from Sam written from Galesburg.
Sam writes that he found the third level, has set up a hay, feed and grain business (his old dream), and urges Charley and Louisa to keep looking.
A first-day cover is an envelope with a new stamp, posted on the first day the stamp is issued; the postmark proves the date.
Twist ending: the first-day cover is evidence that the third level was real, overturning Sam's own theory.
Stamp collecting connects past and present, and the first-day cover becomes the bridge between them.

example.q: Why is the first-day cover important to the story?
steps: Its postmark proves the date: 18 July 1894.
The letter inside is from Sam, who had vanished.
So it proves Sam reached 1894 through the third level.
example.answer: It is dated proof from 1894 that Sam reached the past, so the third level was real.

learn.reallife: India Post issues first-day covers with special cancellations whenever a new stamp comes out. Philatelists value them because the date is certain.

topics.title: Themes: escape, time and nostalgia

learn.hook: Fear, war, worry: Charley's modern world feels heavy. Galesburg, 1894, feels light. Who wouldn't want a door between them?
points: Escapism: Charley wants to escape modern insecurity, war and worry.
Fantasy versus reality: the story keeps us guessing; the corridor, the newspaper and the first-day cover blur the line.
Intersection of time and space: one place (Grand Central) opens onto another time (1894).
Nostalgia: a longing for a peaceful past: big lawns, long summer evenings, people sitting out under trees in Galesburg.
Was the third level a medium of escape? Yes: it was Charley's way out of a stressful present, and later Sam's.

Hero: Maharaja Sir Jilani Jung Jung Bahadur of Pratibandapuram, known as the Tiger King.

learn.reallife: Wildlife officials in India say many tigers were lost to royal hunts in the princely era. Kalki's satire hits a real target.

topics.title: The vow of a hundred tigers

learn.hook: Told that a tiger may kill him, the king decides to kill tigers first, a hundred of them.
points: The prince was raised the 'English' way: an English nurse (nanny) and an English tutor. At twenty he became king.
He killed his first tiger and vowed to kill a hundred. The chief astrologer warned him: he might kill ninety-nine, but he must be careful with the hundredth.
To keep all the tigers for himself, he banned tiger hunting by anyone else in his state.

example.q: Why did the Maharaja ban tiger hunting by others?
steps: He had vowed to kill a hundred tigers himself.
Others hunting would reduce the number left for him.
So he made tiger hunting his own monopoly.
example.answer: To keep all the tigers for himself so he could complete his vow of a hundred kills.

learn.reallife: Today India's Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, bans tiger hunting for everyone, kings included. Kalki's Maharaja banned it only so he could hunt alone.

topics.title: Diamonds for a duchess, brides for tigers

learn.hook: To keep his tigers, the king risks his throne. To keep his throne, he buys diamonds. To find more tigers, he chooses a wife.
points: A high-ranking British officer wanted to hunt a tiger in the state. The king refused, and risked losing his throne.
He saved his kingdom by sending about fifty costly diamond rings to the officer's wife, who chose one or two but kept them all.
Within ten years he had killed seventy tigers, and tigers vanished from his state.
He then married a girl from a state with many tigers, and killed tigers there on each visit to his father-in-law.

topics.title: The hundredth tiger takes its revenge

learn.hook: Ninety-nine down. The last tiger is an old one from a park, and the king's bullet misses. The real hundredth tiger is made of wood.
points: After ninety-nine tigers, none were left. The worried dewan secretly brought an old tiger from the People's Park in Madras and let it loose.
The king's bullet missed. The tiger fainted from shock; the hunters found it alive and killed it secretly, without telling the king.
For his son's third birthday, the king bought a cheap wooden toy tiger, crudely carved. A sliver from it pierced his right hand.
The infection spread; he died during the operation. The hundredth tiger had taken its revenge.

example.q: How is the prophecy fulfilled?

learn.reallife: Doctors in India warn that even a small wooden splinter can cause a serious infection if ignored. Kalki uses this tiny cause for a huge, ironic end.

topics.title: Irony, fate, wildlife and humour

learn.hook: The man who killed ninety-nine real tigers dies because of a wooden one. Irony doesn't get sharper than that.
points: Irony of fate and the inevitability of destiny: the king tries to defeat the prophecy, but it is fulfilled in an unexpected way.
Destruction of wildlife: one man's vanity wipes out tigers from his state and beyond; the story indirectly argues for conservation.
Satire, irony and dramatic irony: readers know the 'hundredth' tiger was killed by hunters while the king celebrates.
Humour and exaggeration (a talking baby, fifty rings, a bride chosen for tigers), with suspense around the hundredth tiger.

example.q: Explain the dramatic irony in the hunt of the old tiger.
steps: Dramatic irony: the reader knows something a character does not.

example.answer: Readers know the king missed and the hunters killed the tiger, while he believes his vow is complete and he is safe.

learn.reallife: Project Tiger, launched in India in 1973, helped tiger numbers recover. Kalki's satire shows the kind of thinking that brought tigers to the edge.

topics.title: From Madras to the bottom of the world

learn.hook: A writer from Madras boards a Russian research ship and sails to the coldest, driest, windiest place on Earth.
points: Author: Tishani Doshi, an Indian poet, journalist and dancer from Madras (Chennai).

The journey: from Madras, crossing nine time zones, six checkpoints, three bodies of water and three ecospheres.
The voyage is aboard the Russian research vessel 'Akademik Shokalskiy'.

topics.title: Gondwana and the Earth's memory in ice

learn.hook: Six hundred and fifty million years ago, India and Antarctica were neighbours in one giant landmass.
points: About 650 million years ago, a giant southern supercontinent, Gondwana, existed, centred roughly around present-day Antarctica.
Gondwana broke up, and the continents, including India, drifted to their present positions.
Antarctica's ice preserves a record of the Earth's past: layers of ice trap air and carbon from ancient times.
So Antarctica is key to understanding the Earth's past, present and future.

example.q: Why is Antarctica the place to understand the Earth's past?
steps: It was once the centre of Gondwana.

These records help scientists read history and predict change.
example.answer: Its ice holds a record of ancient climate and it was the heart of Gondwana, so it tells the Earth's history.

learn.reallife: India was part of Gondwana too. Geologists find similar rocks and fossils, like Glossopteris plants, in India and Antarctica.

topics.title: Melting ice, carbon and the tiny plants that feed an ocean

learn.hook: The smallest living things in the Southern Ocean hold up the whole food chain, including the whales.
points: If the West Antarctic ice sheet melted, sea levels would rise dramatically, threatening coastal lands.
Rising carbon dioxide levels, global warming and the thinning of the ozone layer threaten the planet.
Phytoplankton, the 'grasses of the sea', are single-celled plants that use sunlight to make food by photosynthesis; they nourish and sustain the entire Southern Ocean food chain.
Lesson: small changes can have big effects. Take care of the small things, and the big things will fall into place.

example.q: Why are phytoplankton important?
steps: They are tiny plants that make food by photosynthesis.
Krill and fish feed on them; bigger animals feed on those.
If they decline, the whole food chain suffers.
example.answer: They are the base of the Southern Ocean food chain; damage to them affects every animal above them.

learn.reallife: Coastal cities like Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata are among those studied for sea-level-rise risk. Antarctic ice matters to India directly.

topics.title: Students on Ice: hope for the planet

points: 'Students on Ice' is a programme led by Canadian Geoff Green that takes high school students to Antarctica.

steps: Young people are the future policy-makers.

example.answer: Because students will be tomorrow's decision-makers, and an early, first-hand experience can inspire them to protect the planet.

learn.reallife: Indian teens like the young climate activists who speak at school assemblies and global summits show what Geoff Green's idea can achieve.

topics.title: Dr Sadao's house by the sea

learn.hook: War between Japan and America. A Japanese surgeon trained in America. One misty evening, the war washes up on his beach.
points: Author: Pearl S. Buck, an American writer who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1938.
Setting: Japan during the Second World War, when Japan and the USA were enemies.
Dr Sadao Hoki, a skilled Japanese surgeon trained in America, lives in a house on the Japanese coast with his wife Hana.
His father had valued education and Japan's future. Sadao met Hana in America, and they married in Japan with their families' approval.

learn.reallife: Many Indian doctors train abroad and serve at home, at AIIMS or district hospitals. Medicine crosses borders even when politics divides them.

topics.title: A wounded enemy on the shore

learn.hook: Through the mist, Sadao and Hana see a body on the rocks. The cap says 'U.S. Navy'. What would you do?
points: In the evening mist, Sadao and Hana find a wounded white man washed up on the shore; his cap reads 'U.S. Navy'.
He is an escaped American prisoner of war with a gunshot wound.
Sadao and Hana are torn between patriotism (hand him over) and humanity (save his life). They take him into their house.

example.q: Why are Sadao and Hana torn about what to do?
steps: As patriots, they should hand over an enemy.

example.answer: Their duty to their country clashes with their humanity and Sadao's medical duty, and helping him is dangerous.

learn.reallife: Doctors in conflict zones, like those with the International Committee of the Red Cross, are trained to treat every wounded person, friend or foe.

learn.hook: 'Sadao's dilemma' is the classic long answer from Vistas. Know its two sides, and the marks follow.
points: Sadao's dilemma: duty to his country (hand over the enemy) versus duty as a doctor (save a dying man).
Why the servants left: they believed sheltering an enemy was wrong and dangerous. The General: self-centred, cares only for his own health.
Short answers on Sadao (dedicated, ethical, torn) and Hana (compassionate, supportive).
Long answer on humanity versus patriotism: the discovery, the operation, the General's failed plan, the escape, and the message.

example.q: Write a 50-word answer: What was Sadao's dilemma?
steps: As a patriot, he should hand over an enemy prisoner.
As a doctor, he must save the dying man.
Helping him risked his family's safety.
example.answer: Sadao had to choose between patriotism and humanity. As a loyal Japanese he should hand over the escaped American prisoner, but as a doctor he could not let a wounded man die. Helping him also endangered his family.

learn.reallife: Films and stories often show soldiers or doctors helping a wounded rival. The board exam often asks students to connect such ideas to 'The Enemy'.

chapters.title: Vistas: On the Face of It

topics.title: A burnt face meets a tin leg

learn.hook: A bitter boy climbs a wall into what he thinks is an empty garden. An old man with a tin leg says, 'Come in.'
points: Author: Susan Hill, an English novelist and playwright. 'On the Face of It' is a one-act play in two scenes.
Characters: Derry, a boy of about fourteen; Mr Lamb, an old man; and Derry's mother.
Derry climbs into Mr Lamb's garden thinking it empty. Mr Lamb welcomes him instead of scolding him.
One side of Derry's face was burnt by acid; he is bitter, defensive and withdrawn.
Mr Lamb has a tin leg, lost in a war; children mock him as 'Lamey-Lamb', but he does not mind.

example.q: How do Derry and Mr Lamb first react to each other?
steps: Derry is startled and defensive; he expects disgust.
Mr Lamb is calm and welcoming; he doesn't comment on the face first.
Their contrast sets up the play.
example.answer: Derry is suspicious and defensive, while Mr Lamb is warm and accepting, which disarms him.

learn.reallife: Acid attack survivors in India, like those at Agra's Sheroes Hangout café, show the courage Derry must learn: facing the world without hiding.

topics.title: Crab apples, bees and a picture that fell

learn.hook: Mr Lamb thinks weeds are flowers too. That one idea starts to change how Derry sees himself.
points: The garden: crab apples for making jelly, bees and their honey, weeds and flowers growing together.
Mr Lamb's philosophy: all things in nature are equal (a weed is a flower too); people fear what is different.
Derry recalls overhearing his mother say that only a mother could love a face like his, which hurt him deeply.
Mr Lamb tells of a man who shut himself away for fear of the world and was killed anyway, when a picture fell off his wall.
Derry, touched, promises to come back to help pick the crab apples.

example.q: What is the point of Mr Lamb's story about the man and the picture?
steps: The man hid indoors to stay safe.
He died at home anyway, when a picture fell on him.
So hiding from life does not protect you; it only wastes life.
example.answer: That shutting yourself away out of fear doesn't keep you safe; you might as well live fully.

learn.reallife: Indian kitchens turn fruit into jams and murabbas the way Mr Lamb turns crab apples into jelly: making something sweet from something sour.

topics.title: Scene 2: going back, and finding loss

learn.hook: Derry's mother says no. For the first time, Derry says, 'I'm going.' He gets there too late.
points: At home, Derry's mother forbids him to go back to Mr Lamb, distrusting the old man.
Derry insists: he wants to go out and see the world and things; he will not stay shut away.
He returns to the garden to find Mr Lamb has fallen from the ladder while picking crab apples, and has died. Derry weeps.

example.q: Why is Derry's decision to go back so important?
steps: Earlier he hid from people and the world.
Now he defies his mother to go out.
This shows Mr Lamb's influence has changed him.
example.answer: It shows he has begun to overcome his bitterness and fear, choosing to face the world as Mr Lamb taught.

learn.reallife: Peer support groups in Indian schools help students who feel 'different' to step out. Derry's step out of the house is that same turning point.

topics.title: Derry, Mr Lamb, and living with difference

learn.hook: One is young and bitter; one is old and cheerful. Both carry a visible difference, and both are lonely.
points: Derry: bitter, insecure and defensive at first, but he learns hope and courage from Mr Lamb.
Mr Lamb: wise and cheerful, but lonely; he accepts his tin leg and others' teasing, and keeps his gate open to all.
Theme: disability, loneliness and acceptance. Both are isolated by how others see them; acceptance begins within.

example.q: How does Mr Lamb handle his disability differently from Derry?
steps: Derry hides and feels bitter about his face.
Mr Lamb accepts his tin leg and laughs at teasing.
He keeps his gate open and lives fully.
example.answer: Mr Lamb accepts his disability cheerfully and stays open to life, while Derry hides in bitterness.

learn.reallife: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, in India aims at dignity and inclusion. Mr Lamb's attitude shows what inner acceptance looks like.

topics.title: Friendship, appearance and the play's ending

learn.hook: 'On the face of it' means 'as it seems at first'. The title is a pun, and the play is about looking beneath faces.
points: Friendship across ages: a boy and an old man find understanding; a positive attitude to life is passed from one to the other.
Appearance versus reality: 'on the face of it' means as things first appear; a scarred face or a tin leg hides a whole person beneath.
Form: a one-act play built on dialogue; irony of the ending, as Derry returns, changed and ready to live, only to find Mr Lamb has died.

example.q: Why is the ending ironic?
steps: Mr Lamb taught Derry to stop fearing and start living.
Derry comes back, ready to help and be a friend.
But Mr Lamb, who was full of life, has died in an ordinary accident.
example.answer: Just when Derry has learnt to live and returns as a friend, Mr Lamb, the teacher of that lesson, is gone.

learn.reallife: Inter-generational programmes where students spend time with senior citizens are growing in Indian cities. Derry and Mr Lamb show why they work.

topics.title: Board exam practice: On the Face of It

learn.hook: 'What draws Derry to Mr Lamb?' and 'Will Derry return to his old self?' are favourite board questions.
points: What draws Derry: Mr Lamb treats him normally, doesn't pity or stare, and talks sense about fear and difference.
Mr Lamb's loneliness: open gate, few visitors, talking to bees, children mocking him.
Will Derry return to his old self? Unlikely; he has learnt to face the world, and he weeps for a friend he chose to return to.
Aptness of the title: appearance versus reality; both characters are more than what they look like.
Long answer: attitudes to disability: Derry's bitterness, Mr Lamb's acceptance, society's fear of difference.

example.q: Write a 50-word answer: What draws Derry towards Mr Lamb?
steps: Mr Lamb does not stare at or pity his face.
He speaks to him as an equal and shares wisdom.

example.answer: Mr Lamb treats Derry normally, without staring or pity. He talks to him as an equal, shares his view that all things are equal and that hiding is useless. This acceptance and wisdom draw the lonely, bitter boy towards him.

topics.title: Two childhoods, two continents

learn.hook: One girl in America, one in Tamil Nadu, decades and oceans apart, yet their childhood memories echo each other.
points: The chapter has two autobiographical episodes by women from marginalised communities.
Part 1 is by Zitkala-Sa (Gertrude Simmons Bonnin), a Native American writer. Part 2 is by Bama, a Tamil Dalit writer, from her autobiography 'Karukku'.
Zitkala-Sa recalls her first day at a missionary boarding school for Native American children.
Strict rules: bells rang for everything, the children marched, and meals followed a fixed routine; she felt embarrassed and closely watched in unfamiliar clothes.

example.q: Why are the two accounts placed together?
steps: Both are true stories by women from marginalised groups.
Both describe painful childhood experiences of discrimination.
Together they show oppression is not limited to one culture.
example.answer: Because both show how marginalised children faced discrimination, and how they responded, across very different cultures.

learn.reallife: NCERT pairs these two stories to help students see that injustice can look different in different places but feels similar to those who suffer it.

topics.title: The cutting of her long hair

learn.hook: Her friend whispers a warning: they are going to cut our hair. For Zitkala-Sa, that is worse than any punishment.
points: Her friend Judewin, who knew a little English, warned that the school authorities would cut their long, heavy hair.
In her culture, shingled hair was worn by cowards and short hair by mourners; long hair was a mark of pride.
She decided to resist: she crept upstairs and hid under a bed in a large, dimly lit room.
She was found, dragged out kicking and scratching, tied to a chair, and her long hair was cut. She felt like one of many little animals driven by a herder.
She lost her spirit; no one came to comfort her as her mother would have.

example.q: Why was the cutting of her hair so painful for Zitkala-Sa?
steps: In her culture long hair meant pride and dignity.
Shingled hair marked cowards; short hair marked mourners.
Cutting it by force insulted her identity.
example.answer: Because it stripped her of her cultural identity and dignity, branding her, in her people's eyes, as a coward or mourner.

learn.reallife: In many Indian communities, hair also carries meaning, in rituals, vows and identity. That helps us feel why the forced haircut was such a deep wound.

topics.title: Bama and the packet of vadai

learn.hook: A little girl laughs at an old man carrying a snack by its string. Her brother's explanation changes her life.
points: Bama, in the third grade, takes her time walking home, watching the sights of the street: performers, shops, festivals and the threshing floor.
She sees an elder of her community carrying a small packet of vadai by its string, without touching it, and handing it to the landlord.

She finds it funny at first. Her elder brother, Annan, explains that it is because of untouchability: people of so-called upper castes believe they would be polluted by the touch of people from her community.
Annan tells her that because of the community they are born into, they are denied honour and dignity, but that education can win them respect; she must study hard.
Bama takes his words to heart, studies hard and stands first in her class.

example.q: How does Bama's understanding change after Annan's explanation?
steps: At first she sees only a comic way of carrying a packet.
Annan explains it is caused by untouchability.
She now sees the humiliation behind it and resolves to study.
example.answer: She moves from amusement to painful awareness of caste discrimination, and resolves to win respect through education.

learn.reallife: The Constitution of India abolishes untouchability (Article 17) and makes its practice an offence. Bama's story shows why this protection matters.

topics.title: Themes: identity, caste and the power of education

learn.hook: Two girls, two kinds of oppression, and two forms of resistance: one who fights, one who studies.
points: Cultural oppression and loss of identity: Zitkala-Sa's long hair, language and freedom are taken away by the school.
Casteism and untouchability: Bama sees an elder humiliated by caste practice.
Resistance and the power of education: Zitkala-Sa resists by hiding and struggling; Bama resists by studying and excelling.
Style: first-person narration, vivid sensory detail (the bells, the cold scissors, the street sights), and a parallel drawn between two cultures.

example.q: How do the two narrators resist oppression differently?
steps: Zitkala-Sa resists physically: she hides, kicks and struggles.
Bama resists through education: she studies and stands first.
Both refuse to accept injustice quietly.
example.answer: Zitkala-Sa resists openly and physically, while Bama resists through education; both refuse to accept their oppression.

learn.reallife: Dr B.R. Ambedkar, chief architect of the Indian Constitution, urged people to 'educate, agitate, organise'. Bama's choice reflects the first of those words.

topics.title: Board exam practice: Memories of Childhood

learn.hook: 'What is common to the two accounts?' is almost certain to appear. Here is a clean answer frame.
points: Common features: both are autobiographical, by women from marginalised communities; both describe childhood discrimination; both show resistance.
Responses: Zitkala-Sa fights physically and loses her hair but not her will to resist; Bama channels her pain into education.
Bama's growing understanding: from amusement, to Annan's explanation, to anger, to a resolve to study.
Short answers on each part; long answer on resistance and identity, comparing both narrators.

example.q: Write a 50-word answer: What is common to the two accounts?
steps: Both are true stories by women from marginalised groups.
Both show discrimination in childhood.
Both narrators resist in their own way.
example.answer: Both are autobiographical accounts by women from marginalised communities. Each describes childhood discrimination, cultural in Zitkala-Sa's case and caste-based in Bama's, and each shows resistance: Zitkala-Sa by struggling, Bama by studying hard to win respect.

learn.reallife: Many first-generation learners in India today, the first in their families to reach college, echo Bama's belief that education opens closed doors.
